board_events.text: DISTANCE = the total length of the actual path covered. A scalar. It only ever grows.
DISPLACEMENT = the shortest gap from the initial position to the final position, together with the direction. A vector.
Distance is a plain number. Displacement carries a direction, so in one dimension it carries a $+$ or $-$ sign.
Fix a positive direction FIRST. Without it, a value like $-3$ m/s is meaningless and sign errors cascade.
This single split is the seed the whole topic grows from.

segments.text: <curious>Picture a local train pulling out of Dadar station, looping along the Mumbai coast, and stopping at Bandra. Ask the motorman how far you travelled and he points at the odometer. Now stand at Dadar with a measuring tape and stretch it straight across to Bandra, and you get a much shorter number. Same journey — but these are two genuinely different questions, and physics gives them two different names.

Look at the picture. The blue line is the track the train actually rolled over, every twist of it. The red dashed arrow is that measuring tape, cutting straight from start to finish. Two things to notice. The blue line is obviously longer. And the red arrow has an arrowhead — it points somewhere. The blue line does not point anywhere at all.

That blue path length is distance. It is the total length of the actual path covered, and it has one stubborn habit: it only ever grows. Every metre the train rolls adds to it. It cannot shrink, and it does not care which way you went. That makes it a scalar — a plain number with a unit, no direction attached.

The red arrow is displacement. It is the shortest gap from where you started to where you finished, bundled together with the direction from one to the other. That direction is not decoration; it is part of the quantity itself. Displacement is a vector.

Written down, displacement is beautifully simple: delta x equals x final minus x initial. Endpoints only. This formula does not know and does not care what happened in between — whether the train looped, halted, or reversed. Only the two ends enter the calculation.

Hence the red note. Distance is a plain number. Displacement carries a direction — and in a straight line a direction has only two options, so a sign is all you need. Plus or minus is a complete description of direction here.

Which brings the one rule to lock in before every single problem: fix a positive direction first. Say rightward is positive, or east is positive. Do it before you write anything else down. Skip it and a value like minus three metres per second is literally meaningless, and the sign errors will cascade through your entire solution.

This one split is the seed the whole chapter grows from. From distance and displacement sprout speed and velocity, average and instantaneous, and eventually the whole graphical toolkit. Get this pair clean and everything downstream falls into place.

<curious>ज़रा सोचिए, एक local train Dadar station से निकलती है, Mumbai coast के साथ घूमती हुई Bandra पहुँचती है। Motorman से पूछिए कितना travel किया — वो odometer दिखाएगा। लेकिन अगर आप Dadar पर measuring tape लेकर खड़े हों और सीधा Bandra तक खींचें, तो number बहुत छोटा आएगा। एक ही journey, मगर ये दो बिलकुल अलग questions हैं, और physics इन्हें दो अलग नाम देती है।

Picture देखिए। Blue line वो track है जिस पर train असल में चली — हर मोड़ के साथ। Red dashed arrow वही measuring tape है, start से finish तक सीधा। दो चीज़ें notice कीजिए। Blue line साफ़ तौर पर लंबी है। और red arrow पर arrowhead है — वो कहीं point कर रहा है। Blue line कहीं point नहीं करती।

उस blue path की length को कहते हैं distance। ये actual path की total length है, और इसकी एक ज़िद्दी आदत है: ये सिर्फ़ बढ़ता है। Train का हर metre इसमें जुड़ता जाता है। ये कभी घटता नहीं, और इसे direction से कोई मतलब नहीं। इसीलिए ये एक scalar है — सिर्फ़ number और unit, direction नहीं।

Red arrow है displacement। ये shortest gap है — जहाँ से शुरू किया वहाँ से जहाँ ख़त्म किया — और साथ में direction भी। वो direction कोई सजावट नहीं है, वो quantity का हिस्सा है। इसलिए displacement एक vector है।

Formula में displacement बेहद simple है: delta x equals x final minus x initial. सिर्फ़ endpoints। इस formula को पता ही नहीं कि बीच में क्या हुआ — train घूमी, रुकी, या वापस आई। सिर्फ़ दोनों सिरे calculation में आते हैं।

इसीलिए ये red note. Distance एक plain number है। Displacement direction रखता है — और straight line में direction के सिर्फ़ दो options हैं, तो एक sign ही काफ़ी है। यहाँ plus या minus पूरा direction बता देता है।

और यहीं से वो rule आता है जो हर problem से पहले lock करना है: सबसे पहले positive direction fix कीजिए। मान लीजिए rightward positive है, या east positive है। ये कुछ भी लिखने से पहले करना है। अगर छोड़ दिया, तो minus three metres per second का कोई मतलब ही नहीं बचता, और sign errors पूरे solution में फैल जाते हैं।

यही एक split है जिससे पूरा chapter उगता है। Distance और displacement से speed और velocity निकलते हैं, average और instantaneous निकलते हैं, और आगे चलकर पूरा graphical toolkit। ये pair साफ़ हो गया तो आगे सब अपने आप जगह पर बैठ जाएगा।

sections.title: Speed and velocity: the scalar twin and the vector twin

board_events.text: From one pair, two more pairs sprout
SPEED = rate of change of DISTANCE. Scalar. Always positive.
VELOCITY = rate of change of DISPLACEMENT, with direction. Vector.
Same units (m/s), same dimensions $[LT^{-1}]$ — velocity just also tells you which way.
A speedometer shows SPEED, never velocity: it does not know your direction.

board_events.text: Run there and back: displacement is ZERO, distance is the full 35.36 m.
That gap between them is the heart of kinematics.

segments.text: From that first pair, distance and displacement, two more pairs sprout almost automatically. Because once you have two ways of measuring how far, you get two ways of measuring how fast.
Speed is how fast distance piles up — the rate of change of distance. Since distance only grows, speed is always positive. It is the scalar twin, inheriting scalar-ness from its parent.

Velocity is how fast displacement changes, direction included. It is the rate of change of displacement, and it inherits the vector nature of displacement. So velocity can be negative — that simply means motion in the direction you called negative.

Read the red note carefully, because this is where students get careless. Speed and velocity have the same units, metres per second, and the same dimensions, length times time to the power minus one. They are not different kinds of things dimensionally. The one and only difference is that velocity also tells you which way.

Here is a test you can feel. Your car's speedometer — what does it actually show? Speed. Always positive, always a bare number. It cannot show you velocity, because it has no idea which direction you are pointing. Reverse out of a parking spot and the needle still swings positive.

Now the cricket example, and I want you to watch what happens. A batsman takes a quick single: he sprints from one crease to the other, seventeen point six eight metres down the pitch. That is his displacement so far. But the call gets cancelled, so he scrambles back.

<excited>Watch the two boxes. His distance is seventeen point six eight plus seventeen point six eight — that is thirty five point three six metres, and he is gasping for breath from every one of them. His displacement is plus seventeen point six eight minus seventeen point six eight, which is exactly zero. He is standing where he started.

That is the famous result on the board: a round trip has zero displacement but plenty of distance. Zero displacement does not mean nothing happened. It means the endpoints coincide — and endpoints are the only thing displacement ever looks at.

That gap between the two — distance climbing while displacement sits at zero — is the heart of kinematics. Almost every trap in this chapter is built on a student quietly assuming those two numbers are the same.
उस पहले pair से — distance और displacement — दो और pairs लगभग अपने आप निकल आते हैं। क्योंकि जब कितनी दूर measure करने के दो तरीक़े हैं, तो कितना तेज़ measure करने के भी दो तरीक़े होंगे।

Speed बताता है distance कितनी तेज़ी से जमा हो रहा है — rate of change of distance. और चूँकि distance सिर्फ़ बढ़ता है, speed हमेशा positive होता है। ये scalar twin है, अपने parent से scalar-ness विरासत में लेकर।

Velocity बताता है displacement कितनी तेज़ी से बदल रहा है, direction के साथ। ये rate of change of displacement है, और displacement की vector nature इसे मिलती है। इसीलिए velocity negative हो सकता है — इसका सीधा मतलब है motion उस direction में जिसे आपने negative कहा था।

ये red note ध्यान से पढ़िए, यहीं students लापरवाह हो जाते हैं। Speed और velocity के units एक ही हैं, metres per second, और dimensions भी एक ही, length into time to the power minus one. Dimensionally ये अलग चीज़ें हैं ही नहीं। बस एक ही फ़र्क़ है — velocity ये भी बताता है कि किधर।

एक test जो आप महसूस कर सकते हैं। आपकी car का speedometer असल में दिखाता क्या है? Speed. हमेशा positive, हमेशा सिर्फ़ एक number. वो velocity दिखा ही नहीं सकता, क्योंकि उसे पता ही नहीं आप किस direction में हैं। Parking से reverse लीजिए, needle फिर भी positive ही जाएगी।

अब cricket वाला example, और ध्यान से देखिए क्या होता है। Batsman quick single लेता है: एक crease से दूसरी तक दौड़ता है, seventeen point six eight metres pitch पर। अभी तक यही उसका displacement है। लेकिन call cancel हो जाती है, तो वो वापस भागता है।

<excited>दोनों boxes देखिए। उसका distance है seventeen point six eight plus seventeen point six eight — यानी thirty five point three six metres, और हर metre की साँस फूल रही है। उसका displacement है plus seventeen point six eight minus seventeen point six eight, यानी बिलकुल zero. वो वहीं खड़ा है जहाँ से शुरू किया था।

यही है board पर लिखा famous result: round trip में displacement zero होता है, मगर distance भरपूर। Zero displacement का मतलब ये नहीं कि कुछ हुआ ही नहीं। मतलब ये है कि endpoints एक ही जगह हैं — और displacement सिर्फ़ endpoints ही देखता है।
यही gap — distance बढ़ता जाए और displacement zero पर बैठा रहे — kinematics का दिल है। इस chapter के लगभग सारे traps इसी पर बने हैं कि student चुपचाप मान लेता है दोनों numbers एक ही हैं।

board_events.text: AVERAGE SPEED = total distance / total time. AVERAGE VELOCITY = net displacement / total time.
Both describe the WHOLE journey with a single number. They smear over everything in between.
INSTANTANEOUS velocity = the value at one exact moment — the speed gun clocking a delivery.
At a single instant there is no path left to bend, so instantaneous SPEED $=$ $|$instantaneous velocity$|$ exactly.
That is why the scalar and vector twins finally agree — but only at an instant.

segments.text: So far we have talked about how far. Now zoom in on time, because the same quantity gives you two very different answers depending on how wide a time window you look through.

The picture shows both. The blue bracket spans the entire journey, start to finish — that is the average view. The red dot is a single moment, one instant, with the window collapsed to a point — that is the instantaneous view. Same motion; two completely different questions being asked of it.

Over a whole journey we take averages. Average speed is total distance over total time. Average velocity is net displacement over total time. Notice which numerator each one takes — average speed inherits from distance, average velocity inherits from displacement. That inheritance is the whole game.

And here is what averages honestly are: they describe the entire journey with one single number. They smear over everything in between. The train may have halted, sprinted, reversed — the average tells you none of it. It is a summary, not a description.

But sometimes you need the value right now. The speed gun clocking a bowler's delivery does not want the average over his run-up. It wants this exact moment. That is the instantaneous value, and getting it requires a genuinely new idea.

Here is that idea on the board. Take the average over an interval delta t, then shrink the interval down toward nothing. As delta t goes to zero, the ratio delta x over delta t settles on a definite value — and that limit is the derivative, d x by d t. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time. That is why calculus enters this chapter at all.

Now the red note, and it is a quietly lovely result. At a single instant there is no path left to bend. There is no room for the route to wander away from the straight gap, because there is no interval. So the instantaneous speed is exactly the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity — not approximately, exactly.

That is when the scalar and vector twins finally agree perfectly. But hold on to the condition: only at an instant. Stretch it into any interval at all, and the moment the path bends or reverses, they part ways again.
अब तक हमने बात की कितनी दूर की। अब time पर zoom कीजिए, क्योंकि वही quantity आपको दो बहुत अलग जवाब देती है — ये इस पर depend करता है कि आप कितनी चौड़ी time window से देख रहे हैं।

Picture में दोनों हैं। Blue bracket पूरी journey पर फैला है, start से finish तक — ये average वाला view है। Red dot एक single moment है, एक instant, जहाँ window सिकुड़कर point बन गई — ये instantaneous view है। Motion एक ही, मगर सवाल बिलकुल अलग।

पूरी journey पर हम averages लेते हैं। Average speed होता है total distance over total time. Average velocity होता है net displacement over total time. ध्यान दीजिए numerator किसका है — average speed distance से आया है, average velocity displacement से। यही inheritance पूरा खेल है।

और averages असल में हैं क्या: वो पूरी journey को एक ही number में समेट देते हैं। बीच का सब कुछ smear हो जाता है। Train रुकी, दौड़ी, वापस आई — average कुछ नहीं बताएगा। ये एक summary है, description नहीं।

लेकिन कभी-कभी आपको अभी की value चाहिए। Speed gun जो bowler की delivery clock करती है, उसे run-up का average नहीं चाहिए। उसे यही exact moment चाहिए। यही instantaneous value है, और इसे निकालने के लिए एक बिलकुल नया idea चाहिए।

वो idea board पर है। एक interval delta t पर average लीजिए, फिर interval को सिकोड़ते जाइए। जैसे delta t zero की तरफ़ जाता है, ratio delta x over delta t एक definite value पर आकर बैठ जाता है — और वही limit derivative है, d x by d t. Instantaneous velocity यानी position का time के साथ derivative. इसीलिए इस chapter में calculus घुसती है।

अब red note, और ये चुपचाप बहुत ख़ूबसूरत result है। एक single instant पर path के मुड़ने की जगह ही नहीं बचती। Route को straight gap से भटकने का मौक़ा नहीं मिलता, क्योंकि interval ही नहीं है। इसलिए instantaneous speed बिलकुल instantaneous velocity का magnitude है — approximately नहीं, exactly.

यही वो पल है जब scalar और vector twins पूरी तरह agree करते हैं। लेकिन condition याद रखिए: सिर्फ़ instant पर। ज़रा सा भी interval खींचिए, और जहाँ path मुड़ा या reverse हुआ, वहीं दोनों फिर अलग हो जाते हैं।

sections.title: Chord to tangent: why instantaneous velocity is a derivative

board_events.text: The one piece of real reasoning here
Start with average velocity over an interval: $v_{avg} = \Delta x / \Delta t$.

board_events.text: STEP 1: on an $x$-$t$ graph, that ratio is rise over run — the SLOPE of the chord joining A and B.
STEP 2: squeeze the interval. Let B slide toward A, so $\Delta t \to 0$. The chord pivots until it just kisses the curve.
STEP 3: that limiting line is the TANGENT, and its slope is the instantaneous velocity.
This is WHY we use calculus: velocity at an instant is the limiting slope as the measuring window collapses to a point.

segments.text: There is no single grand derivation in this sub-topic, but there is one piece of genuine reasoning that matters, and it is the bridge from average to instantaneous. Let us walk it properly, because if you understand this you never have to memorise the derivative definition again.
Start where we already are. Average velocity over an interval is delta x over delta t — change in position divided by the time it took. Nothing new yet. This is the definition we have had all along.

Now put it on a position-time graph, and watch the picture. The blue curve is the motion. Point A and point B are two moments on it. The red dashed line joins them — that is the chord, sometimes called the secant. The green line touches the curve at A only — that is the tangent. Everything follows from comparing those two lines.

Step one. Look at the grey dashed lines. The horizontal one is the run, which is delta t. The vertical one is the rise, which is delta x. And rise over run is exactly what we mean by slope. So delta x over delta t — our average velocity — is precisely the slope of the chord from A to B. Average velocity is not like a slope. It is a slope.

Step two, and this is the move. Squeeze the interval. Look at the orange arrow at the bottom: slide B along the curve toward A, so delta t shrinks toward zero. As B travels in, the chord has to pivot — it swings around, getting closer and closer to the curve near A, until in the limit it stops cutting through and instead just kisses the curve at that one point.

Step three. That limiting line is the tangent at A, drawn in green. And since the chord's slope was the average velocity all along, the tangent's slope is what the average velocity converges to as the window collapses. That is the instantaneous velocity at A. The chord became the tangent, and the average became the instantaneous.

Which is exactly the line on the board: v equals the limit as delta t goes to zero of delta x over delta t, and that limit is d x by d t. This is not a definition handed to you from nowhere. It is the honest end point of squeezing a chord.

And now the red note answers the question students always ask — why does calculus turn up in a chapter about trains and joggers? Because velocity at an instant is a limiting slope, and a limiting slope is what a derivative is. Calculus is not bolted onto kinematics. Kinematics is where calculus was born.

इस sub-topic में कोई एक बड़ी grand derivation नहीं है, मगर एक genuine reasoning ज़रूर है जो मायने रखती है — average से instantaneous तक का पुल। इसे ठीक से चलिए, क्योंकि ये समझ गए तो derivative की definition दोबारा कभी रटनी नहीं पड़ेगी।
वहीं से शुरू करते हैं जहाँ हम हैं। किसी interval पर average velocity है delta x over delta t — position का change बटा वो time जो लगा। अभी तक कुछ नया नहीं। यही definition हमारे पास पहले से है।

अब इसे position-time graph पर रखिए और picture देखिए। Blue curve motion है। Point A और point B उस पर दो moments हैं। Red dashed line उन्हें जोड़ती है — यही chord है, जिसे secant भी कहते हैं। Green line curve को सिर्फ़ A पर छूती है — यही tangent है। सब कुछ इन्हीं दो lines की तुलना से निकलेगा।

Step one. Grey dashed lines देखिए। Horizontal वाली run है, यानी delta t. Vertical वाली rise है, यानी delta x. और rise over run का मतलब ही slope होता है। तो delta x over delta t — हमारी average velocity — बिलकुल A से B तक की chord का slope है। Average velocity slope जैसी नहीं है। वो slope है।

Step two, और यही असली चाल है। Interval को दबाइए। नीचे orange arrow देखिए: B को curve पर A की तरफ़ खिसकाइए, ताकि delta t zero की तरफ़ सिकुड़े। जैसे-जैसे B अंदर आता है, chord को pivot करना पड़ता है — वो घूमती है, A के पास curve के और क़रीब आती जाती है, और limit में वो curve को काटना छोड़कर सिर्फ़ उस एक point पर छू लेती है।

Step three. वही limiting line A पर tangent है, green में खिंची हुई। और चूँकि chord का slope शुरू से average velocity था, tangent का slope वही है जिस पर average velocity converge करती है जब window सिकुड़ जाए। यही A पर instantaneous velocity है। Chord tangent बन गई, और average instantaneous बन गया।

और board पर यही line है: v equals limit as delta t goes to zero of delta x over delta t, और वो limit है d x by d t. ये कोई definition नहीं जो कहीं से थमा दी गई हो। ये chord को दबाने का ईमानदार अंत है।

अब red note उस सवाल का जवाब देता है जो students हमेशा पूछते हैं — trains और joggers के chapter में calculus आई कहाँ से? क्योंकि instant पर velocity एक limiting slope है, और limiting slope ही तो derivative है। Calculus kinematics पर ऊपर से चिपकाई नहीं गई। Kinematics वो जगह है जहाँ calculus पैदा हुई।

sections.title: Acceleration, retardation, and the zero-velocity trap

board_events.text: Acceleration is NOT just 'speeding up'
ACCELERATION = rate of change of VELOCITY.
Velocity can change in MAGNITUDE (speeding up, slowing down) or in DIRECTION. Either one is acceleration.
When acceleration points OPPOSITE to velocity, the body slows. That is RETARDATION (deceleration).

board_events.text: 'Zero velocity' does NOT mean 'zero acceleration'.
At the top of a thrown ball's flight $v = 0$, but $a = g$ downward. Velocity and acceleration are independent at an instant.

segments.text: Finally, acceleration. And I want to attack the definition head on, because the everyday meaning of the word is actively misleading you before we even begin.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Not the rate of change of speed. Velocity. That distinction is doing enormous work, and we will unpack it in a moment.

The board shows both flavours, and they mirror the velocity pair exactly. Average acceleration is v two minus v one over t two minus t one — a change in velocity over the interval it took. Instantaneous acceleration is d v by d t. And since velocity was already d x by d t, acceleration is the second derivative of position, d squared x by d t squared. Same ladder, one rung further down.

Now here is why 'rate of change of velocity' matters. Velocity is a vector, so it can change in two completely separate ways. It can change in magnitude — you speed up, you slow down. Or it can change in direction while its magnitude stays put. Either one is a change in velocity, so either one is acceleration. Acceleration is not just speeding up. Slowing down is acceleration. Turning at constant speed is acceleration.

And when acceleration points in exactly the opposite direction to velocity, the body slows. That case has its own name — retardation, or deceleration. But notice it is not a different quantity. It is ordinary acceleration wearing a minus sign relative to the motion.

Now the picture, and this is the trap that costs marks every single year. A ball is thrown straight up. It rises, slows, and for one instant at the very top it hangs — velocity is genuinely zero there. Look at the blue box on the diagram.

<whisper>And here is what students do: they see velocity is zero and conclude acceleration must be zero too. Look at the red arrow. It has not shrunk at all. Gravity is still pulling with its full strength, g downward, at the exact instant the ball is motionless.

So the ball does not hang weightless at the top — it is about to fall, and it is being accelerated the whole time it looks still. The lesson generalises well beyond this one example: velocity and acceleration are independent at an instant. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other. A body can have zero velocity and huge acceleration, or huge velocity and zero acceleration.
आख़िर में acceleration। और मैं इस definition पर सीधा हमला करना चाहती हूँ, क्योंकि इस शब्द का रोज़मर्रा वाला मतलब शुरू होने से पहले ही आपको गुमराह कर रहा है।
Acceleration है rate of change of velocity. Speed का rate of change नहीं। Velocity का। यही distinction बहुत बड़ा काम कर रही है, और अभी हम इसे खोलेंगे।

Board पर दोनों flavours हैं, और ये velocity वाले pair का hubahu mirror हैं। Average acceleration है v two minus v one over t two minus t one — interval में velocity का change. Instantaneous acceleration है d v by d t. और चूँकि velocity पहले ही d x by d t थी, acceleration position का second derivative है, d squared x by d t squared. वही सीढ़ी, बस एक step नीचे।

अब समझिए कि rate of change of velocity क्यों मायने रखता है। Velocity एक vector है, तो वो दो बिलकुल अलग तरीक़ों से बदल सकती है। Magnitude में बदल सकती है — आप तेज़ हुए, आप धीमे हुए। या direction में बदल सकती है जबकि magnitude वहीं की वहीं रहे। दोनों ही velocity का change हैं, तो दोनों ही acceleration हैं। Acceleration सिर्फ़ तेज़ होना नहीं है। धीमा होना भी acceleration है। Constant speed पर मुड़ना भी acceleration है।

और जब acceleration velocity के बिलकुल उल्टे direction में हो, तो body धीमी पड़ती है। इस case का अपना नाम है — retardation, या deceleration. लेकिन ध्यान दीजिए, ये कोई अलग quantity नहीं है। ये वही ordinary acceleration है, बस motion के मुक़ाबले minus sign पहने हुए।

अब picture, और यही वो trap है जो हर साल marks खाता है। एक ball सीधा ऊपर फेंकी गई। वो उठती है, धीमी होती है, और बिलकुल ऊपर एक instant के लिए ठहर जाती है — वहाँ velocity सच में zero है। Diagram पर blue box देखिए।

<whisper>और students करते क्या हैं: velocity zero देखकर मान लेते हैं acceleration भी zero होगा। Red arrow देखिए। वो ज़रा भी छोटा नहीं हुआ। जिस exact instant पर ball रुकी हुई है, gravity पूरी ताक़त से खींच रही है, g downward.

तो ball ऊपर weightless लटकी नहीं है — वो गिरने ही वाली है, और जितनी देर वो स्थिर दिखती है उतनी देर भी accelerate हो रही है। ये सबक़ इस एक example से कहीं आगे जाता है: instant पर velocity और acceleration independent हैं। एक को जानकर दूसरे के बारे में कुछ पता नहीं चलता। Body की velocity zero और acceleration ज़बरदस्त हो सकती है, या velocity ज़बरदस्त और acceleration zero.

sections.title: The two inequalities that never break

board_events.text: Limiting conditions you can lean on
Everything in this sub-topic lives in ONE DIMENSION — motion along a straight line. Direction reduces to $+$ or $-$.

board_events.text: EQUALITY holds only for motion along a straight line WITHOUT reversing direction.
The second inequality is the first one divided by the same total time — so it is not a new fact.
Use these as free sanity checks: if your distance comes out smaller than your displacement, you slipped a sign.

segments.text: Before we start calculating, let us collect the fences — the limiting conditions and the two inequalities that this whole sub-topic runs on. These are not decoration. They are free checks on every answer you will ever produce here.

First fence: everything in this sub-topic, as we are teaching it, lives in one dimension. Motion along a straight line. That is a genuine restriction and it buys you something valuable — a direction stops being an arrow in space and reduces to a simple plus or minus sign, once you have fixed a positive direction.

Second: distance is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement. Always. Never the other way round, not once, not for any motion. The path from A to B can be longer than the straight gap, or exactly as long, but it can never be shorter. There is no shortcut shorter than the shortcut.

Third, and it follows immediately: average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity. Look at why. Average speed is distance over total time; average velocity is displacement over the same total time. Same denominator. So dividing the first inequality by that shared total time hands you the second one for free.

Now when does the equal sign actually fire? The picture answers it. On the green side, the motion is straight and one-directional — never turns around. The path never wanders off the straight gap, so distance and the magnitude of displacement are literally the same number, and the two averages match too.

On the red side, the body goes out and comes partly back. The instant it reverses, distance keeps adding while displacement starts subtracting, and the two numbers part company forever. So the condition is precise: straight line, no reversal. That is the one and only case where the twins agree over an interval.

The red note is worth internalising so you do not memorise two separate facts. The second inequality is just the first one divided by the same total time. Learn the distance one properly and the speed one is automatic.

And use them, actively. If you finish a problem and your distance is smaller than your magnitude of displacement, you have not discovered new physics — you have slipped a sign somewhere. Same if average speed comes out below the magnitude of average velocity. These inequalities catch errors for free, before the examiner catches them for you.
Calculation शुरू करने से पहले चलिए बाड़ें इकट्ठी कर लें — वो limiting conditions और दो inequalities जिन पर ये पूरा sub-topic चलता है। ये सजावट नहीं हैं। ये हर answer पर मुफ़्त के checks हैं।

पहली बाड़: इस sub-topic में हम जो पढ़ा रहे हैं वो सब एक dimension में है। Straight line पर motion. ये एक असली restriction है और इसके बदले कुछ क़ीमती मिलता है — direction space में arrow होना छोड़कर सिर्फ़ plus या minus sign बन जाता है, बशर्ते आपने positive direction fix कर लिया हो।

दूसरी: distance हमेशा displacement के magnitude से बड़ा या बराबर होता है। हमेशा। कभी उल्टा नहीं, एक बार भी नहीं, किसी भी motion में नहीं। A से B तक का path straight gap से लंबा हो सकता है, या बिलकुल बराबर, मगर छोटा कभी नहीं। Shortcut से छोटा कोई shortcut होता ही नहीं।

तीसरी, और ये तुरंत निकल आती है: average speed हमेशा average velocity के magnitude से बड़ा या बराबर होता है। वजह देखिए। Average speed है distance over total time; average velocity है displacement over उसी total time. Denominator एक ही। तो पहली inequality को उसी shared total time से divide कीजिए और दूसरी मुफ़्त में मिल जाती है।

अब equal sign कब लगता है? Picture जवाब देती है। Green side पर motion straight है और एक ही direction में — कभी मुड़ता नहीं। Path straight gap से भटकता ही नहीं, तो distance और displacement का magnitude literally एक ही number हैं, और दोनों averages भी बराबर।

Red side पर body बाहर जाती है और आंशिक रूप से वापस आती है। जिस instant वो reverse हुई, distance जुड़ता रहा और displacement घटने लगा, और दोनों numbers हमेशा के लिए अलग हो गए। तो condition बिलकुल सटीक है: straight line, कोई reversal नहीं। किसी interval पर twins के agree करने का यही एकमात्र case है।
Red note समझ लीजिए ताकि दो अलग facts याद न रखने पड़ें। दूसरी inequality पहली को उसी total time से divide करने पर मिलती है। Distance वाली ठीक से सीख लीजिए, speed वाली अपने आप आ जाएगी।

और इन्हें इस्तेमाल कीजिए, actively. अगर problem ख़त्म करने पर आपका distance displacement के magnitude से छोटा है, तो आपने नई physics नहीं खोजी — आपसे कहीं sign फिसला है। यही अगर average speed, average velocity के magnitude से नीचे आ जाए। ये inequalities errors मुफ़्त में पकड़ती हैं, इससे पहले कि examiner आपको पकड़े।

sections.title: Procedure A: a 1-D trip with reversals

board_events.text: Distance vs displacement, step by step
STEP 1: fix a positive direction. Say rightward $=$ $+$.
STEP 2: split the journey into LEGS — stretches where the direction of motion does not change.

board_events.text: STEP 3: DISPLACEMENT = algebraic sum of the legs, respecting $+/-$ signs. Equivalently $x_{final} - x_{initial}$.
STEP 4: DISTANCE = sum of the MAGNITUDES of all legs. Drop the signs.
STEP 5: sanity check. Distance must be $\geq$ $|$displacement$|$. If not, you slipped a sign.
Same legs, added two different ways. That is the whole procedure.

segments.text: Let us turn all that understanding into a procedure you can run without hesitation — the one for handling a one-dimensional trip where the body turns around. Five steps, and the fifth one is free marks.

Step one, and you already know it: fix a positive direction. Rightward is plus, or east is plus, whatever suits the problem. Write it down at the top of your working. This is the step students skip because it feels trivial, and it is exactly the step whose absence wrecks the rest.

Step two. Split the journey into legs. A leg is a stretch where the direction of motion does not change — the body is going one way for the whole of it. Every time the body turns around, that is a new leg. This chopping is what makes the rest mechanical instead of clever.

Look at the picture. The trip has two legs. The blue one runs three hundred metres in the positive direction. The red one comes back one hundred metres in the negative direction. Two legs, because the direction changed exactly once. Both are now written with their sign attached, which is what step one bought us.

Step three. Displacement is the algebraic sum of the legs — you keep every sign. Plus three hundred plus minus one hundred gives plus two hundred metres. And there is a shortcut worth knowing: this must always equal x final minus x initial, the endpoints. If your leg sum and your endpoint difference disagree, one of them is wrong.

Step four. Distance is the sum of the magnitudes of all the legs. Drop every sign. The magnitude of plus three hundred is three hundred, the magnitude of minus one hundred is one hundred, and they add to four hundred metres. Notice how the minus sign, which subtracted in step three, now adds instead. That is the entire difference between the two quantities, in one line.

Step five, the red note, and please actually do this one. Distance must come out greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement. Four hundred against two hundred — passes. If it ever fails, you have not found an exception to physics; you slipped a sign somewhere in steps three or four.

And that is the whole procedure. Same legs, added two different ways: once respecting the signs, once ignoring them. Everything else in this sub-topic that looks like a distance-versus-displacement problem is this procedure wearing a costume.
अब उस पूरी समझ को एक procedure में बदलते हैं जिसे आप बिना अटके चला सकें — एक-dimensional trip के लिए जहाँ body मुड़ती है। पाँच steps, और पाँचवाँ मुफ़्त के marks है।

Step one, जो आप जानते हैं: positive direction fix कीजिए। Rightward plus, या east plus, जो problem को suit करे। इसे working के सबसे ऊपर लिखिए। यही वो step है जिसे students मामूली समझकर छोड़ देते हैं, और यही वो step है जिसकी ग़ैरहाज़िरी बाक़ी सब बिगाड़ देती है।

Step two. Journey को legs में तोड़िए। Leg वो stretch है जिसमें motion का direction नहीं बदलता — body पूरे वक़्त एक ही तरफ़ जा रही है। जब भी body मुड़े, वहाँ नया leg शुरू। यही कटाई बाक़ी काम को चतुराई की जगह mechanical बना देती है।

Picture देखिए। Trip में दो legs हैं। Blue वाला three hundred metres positive direction में। Red वाला one hundred metres negative direction में वापस। दो legs, क्योंकि direction ठीक एक बार बदला। दोनों अब sign के साथ लिखे हैं — यही step one ने हमें दिलाया था।

Step three. Displacement legs का algebraic sum है — हर sign रखिए। Plus three hundred plus minus one hundred, यानी plus two hundred metres. और एक shortcut जानने लायक़ है: ये हमेशा x final minus x initial के बराबर होना चाहिए, यानी endpoints. अगर leg sum और endpoint difference अलग आएँ, तो दोनों में से एक ग़लत है।

Step four. Distance सारे legs के magnitudes का sum है। हर sign गिरा दीजिए। Plus three hundred का magnitude three hundred, minus one hundred का magnitude one hundred, जोड़कर four hundred metres. ग़ौर कीजिए वही minus sign जो step three में घटा रहा था, अब जोड़ रहा है। दोनों quantities का पूरा फ़र्क़ बस इसी एक line में है।

Step five, red note, और ये सच में कीजिए। Distance, displacement के magnitude से बड़ा या बराबर आना चाहिए। Four hundred बनाम two hundred — pass. अगर ये कभी fail हो जाए, तो आपने physics का exception नहीं ढूँढा; आपसे step three या four में कहीं sign फिसला है।

और यही पूरा procedure है। वही legs, दो अलग तरीक़ों से जोड़े गए: एक बार signs के साथ, एक बार signs को नज़रअंदाज़ करके। इस sub-topic में distance-versus-displacement जैसा दिखने वाला बाक़ी सब यही procedure है, भेस बदलकर।

sections.title: Procedure B: is the data 'by distance' or 'by time'?

board_events.text: The one question that decides everything
STEP 1: identify whether the equal pieces are equal DISTANCES or equal TIMES. This decides the whole problem.
STEP 2: always return to first principles — $v_{avg} = $ total distance / total time.

board_events.caption: Equal distances give the harmonic mean; equal times give the arithmetic mean

board_events.text: EQUAL DISTANCES: total time is $\sum d/v_i$. The slow leg hogs the clock and drags the average DOWN.
EQUAL TIMES: total distance is $\sum v_i t$. Each speed gets equal say, so they weigh the same.
Quick check: the average must lie between the smallest and largest speed. For equal distances it sits closer to the SLOWER one.
Never memorise the two results without this reasoning. Derive them in five seconds from first principles instead.

segments.text: Now the second procedure, and it defends you against what the source calls the single most-tested trap in this sub-topic. Two speeds, one average, and everything hinges on a question most students never stop to ask.

Step one is that question: are the equal pieces equal distances, or equal times? Half the route at forty and half at sixty is equal distances. Half the time at forty and half at sixty is equal times. Same words, almost — completely different answers. Read the question for this before you compute anything.

Step two. Whatever the problem says, always come back to first principles. Average speed is total distance over total time. That single line is not a formula to remember alongside the others; it is the definition that generates all of them. If you can only hold one thing, hold this.
Now look at the two panels and let us reason each one out, because I do not want you memorising these results.

Left panel, equal distances. Each half is the same length d, but the slow half at v one takes longer to complete than the fast half at v two. Total time is d over v one plus d over v two. And here is the physical punchline: the slow leg hogs the clock. You spend more of your journey going slowly than going quickly, so the slow speed gets more weight, and the average is dragged down. That is why the answer is the harmonic mean, two v one v two over v one plus v two.

Right panel, equal times. Now each speed gets exactly the same slice of the clock — that is what equal times means. Total distance is v one t plus v two t. Neither speed can hog anything, because the clock is shared evenly. They weigh the same, so the average is the plain arithmetic mean, v one plus v two over two.

The red note gives you two free checks. First, the average must land between the smallest and largest speed — if it does not, you have made an arithmetic error, not a physics discovery. Second, for equal distances it must sit closer to the slower speed. Forty and sixty giving forty eight passes both checks. Forty and sixty giving fifty would fail the second.

So please do not memorise these two results as a pair of formulas to confuse under exam pressure. Ask which pieces are equal, go to total distance over total time, and the right mean falls out in five seconds. The students who memorise are exactly the ones who pick the wrong one when the clock is running.

अब दूसरा procedure, और ये आपको उस चीज़ से बचाता है जिसे source इस sub-topic का सबसे ज़्यादा test होने वाला trap कहता है। दो speeds, एक average, और सब कुछ उस सवाल पर टिका है जो ज़्यादातर students पूछते ही नहीं।

Step one वही सवाल है: बराबर टुकड़े equal distances हैं या equal times? आधा route forty पर और आधा sixty पर — ये equal distances है। आधा time forty पर और आधा sixty पर — ये equal times है। शब्द लगभग एक जैसे, जवाब बिलकुल अलग। कुछ भी compute करने से पहले question में यही पढ़िए।

Step two. Problem कुछ भी कहे, हमेशा first principles पर लौटिए। Average speed equals total distance over total time. ये एक line बाक़ी formulas के साथ याद रखने वाली चीज़ नहीं है; ये वो definition है जो उन सबको पैदा करती है। अगर सिर्फ़ एक चीज़ पकड़नी हो, तो यही पकड़िए।
अब दोनों panels देखिए और हर एक को reason कीजिए, क्योंकि मैं नहीं चाहती आप ये results रटें।

बाएँ panel में equal distances. हर half की length वही d है, मगर v one वाला slow half, v two वाले fast half से ज़्यादा वक़्त लेता है। Total time है d over v one plus d over v two. और physical punchline ये है: slow leg घड़ी हड़प लेता है। आप journey का ज़्यादा हिस्सा धीरे चलने में बिताते हैं, तो slow speed को ज़्यादा weight मिलता है, और average नीचे खिंच जाता है। इसीलिए answer harmonic mean है, two v one v two over v one plus v two.

दाएँ panel में equal times. अब हर speed को घड़ी का बिलकुल बराबर हिस्सा मिलता है — equal times का मतलब ही यही है। Total distance है v one t plus v two t. कोई speed कुछ हड़प नहीं सकती, क्योंकि घड़ी बराबर बँटी है। दोनों का weight एक, तो average सीधा arithmetic mean है, v one plus v two over two.

Red note दो मुफ़्त checks देता है। पहला, average सबसे छोटी और सबसे बड़ी speed के बीच आना चाहिए — नहीं आया तो आपने arithmetic error की है, physics की खोज नहीं। दूसरा, equal distances में वो slower speed के क़रीब बैठना चाहिए। Forty और sixty से forty eight दोनों checks pass करता है। Forty और sixty से fifty दूसरा check fail कर देता।

तो please इन दोनों results को formulas की जोड़ी की तरह मत रटिए, वरना exam pressure में गड्डमड्ड हो जाएँगे। पूछिए कौन से टुकड़े बराबर हैं, total distance over total time पर जाइए, और सही mean पाँच seconds में निकल आएगा। जो रटते हैं, वही घड़ी चलते वक़्त ग़लत वाला उठाते हैं।

sections.title: The kinematic quantities: symbols, units, dimensions

board_events.text: The definitions table — commit it whole
DISTANCE $s$, in m, dimension $[L]$ — total path length, scalar, never negative.
DISPLACEMENT $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$, in m, dimension $[L]$ — change in position, vector.
Both averages: m/s, dimension $[LT^{-1}]$.
Acceleration: m/s$^2$, dimension $[LT^{-2}]$. Note the single power of $T$ in velocity, the square in acceleration.
Speed and velocity are dimensionally IDENTICAL. Dimensions cannot tell scalars from vectors.

segments.text: This section is the reference table, and I want you to hold it as a whole rather than as seven loose facts. Every row has a definition, a symbol, a unit, and a dimensional formula, and the pattern across the rows is the thing worth seeing.

Distance, symbol s, measured in metres, dimension length. It is the total path length, it is a scalar, and it is never negative. That last clause is a definition, not an observation — a negative distance is not a wrong answer, it is a meaningless one.

Displacement, delta x equals x final minus x initial, also in metres, also dimension length. Change in position, and a vector. Notice that distance and displacement have identical units and identical dimensions. They are different quantities that a dimensional check cannot tell apart — which is exactly why you have to keep them straight by meaning.

The two averages. Average speed is total distance over total time. Average velocity is displacement over the time interval. Look at the numerators: one takes the scalar parent, one takes the vector parent. The denominator is identical. Everything that separates these two lives in the numerator.
Both averages come out in metres per second, dimension length times time to the power minus one. Again identical. Dimensions will not save you here either.

The instantaneous pair. Instantaneous velocity is d x by d t — the derivative we built from the chord and the tangent. And instantaneous speed is the magnitude of that same derivative, the modulus of d x by d t. Not a separate calculation. Take the velocity and strip the sign.

Acceleration is d v by d t, which since velocity was already the first derivative of position makes it d squared x by d t squared. Both forms are on the board because problems hand you both — sometimes you have velocity as a function of time, sometimes you have position, and you differentiate once or twice accordingly.

The red note pins the units. Acceleration is metres per second squared, dimension length times time to the power minus two. And notice the pattern that makes this memorable rather than arbitrary: velocity carries a single power of time in the denominator, acceleration carries the square. Each trip down the ladder costs you one more power of time.

One last thing, and it is the trap this table sets. Speed and velocity are dimensionally identical. So are distance and displacement. A dimensional check will never catch you for confusing them, because dimensions simply cannot tell a scalar from a vector. Only meaning can.

ये section reference table है, और मैं चाहती हूँ आप इसे एक पूरी चीज़ की तरह पकड़ें, सात अलग-अलग facts की तरह नहीं। हर row में एक definition है, एक symbol, एक unit, और एक dimensional formula — और rows के आर-पार जो pattern है, असल में वही देखने लायक़ है।

Distance, symbol s, metres में, dimension length. ये total path length है, scalar है, और कभी negative नहीं होता। ये आख़िरी बात definition है, observation नहीं — negative distance ग़लत answer नहीं है, वो बेमानी answer है।

Displacement, delta x equals x final minus x initial, ये भी metres में, dimension भी length. Position का change, और vector. ग़ौर कीजिए distance और displacement के units और dimensions बिलकुल एक जैसे हैं। ये अलग quantities हैं जिन्हें dimensional check पहचान ही नहीं सकता — इसीलिए इन्हें meaning से अलग रखना पड़ता है।

दोनों averages. Average speed है total distance over total time. Average velocity है displacement over time interval. Numerators देखिए: एक scalar parent से आया, दूसरा vector parent से। Denominator बिलकुल एक। इन दोनों को अलग करने वाली हर चीज़ numerator में रहती है।
दोनों averages आते हैं metres per second में, dimension length into time to the power minus one. फिर वही, बिलकुल एक जैसे। यहाँ भी dimensions आपको नहीं बचाएँगे।

Instantaneous pair. Instantaneous velocity है d x by d t — वही derivative जो हमने chord और tangent से बनाया था। और instantaneous speed उसी derivative का magnitude है, modulus of d x by d t. कोई अलग calculation नहीं। Velocity लीजिए और sign हटा दीजिए।

Acceleration है d v by d t, और चूँकि velocity पहले ही position का first derivative थी, ये बन जाता है d squared x by d t squared. दोनों forms board पर हैं क्योंकि problems दोनों देती हैं — कभी velocity time के function के रूप में मिलती है, कभी position, और उसी हिसाब से आप एक बार या दो बार differentiate करते हैं।

Red note units पक्के करता है। Acceleration है metres per second squared, dimension length into time to the power minus two. और वो pattern देखिए जो इसे मनमाना नहीं, यादगार बनाता है: velocity denominator में time की एक power रखती है, acceleration square. सीढ़ी से हर एक क़दम नीचे उतरने की क़ीमत है time की एक और power.

आख़िरी बात, और यही इस table का बिछाया हुआ trap है। Speed और velocity dimensionally बिलकुल एक जैसे हैं। Distance और displacement भी। इन्हें confuse करने पर dimensional check आपको कभी नहीं पकड़ेगा, क्योंकि dimensions scalar और vector में फ़र्क़ कर ही नहीं सकते। सिर्फ़ meaning कर सकती है।

sections.title: Core relations and the two averaging results

board_events.text: The core relations

board_events.latex: v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}, \qquad v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}

board_events.text: Notice the symmetry: each average is a difference over a difference; each instantaneous value is that ratio in the limit.
Two special-case averaging results

board_events.latex: \text{equal distances at } v_1, v_2:\quad v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2} \quad (\text{harmonic mean})
\text{equal times at } v_1, v_2:\quad v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{v_1+v_2}{2} \quad (\text{arithmetic mean})

board_events.text: Memorise the DISTINCTION, not the formulas. This is the single most-tested trap in the sub-topic.

segments.text: Now the core relations, gathered in one place. This is your working toolkit for the sub-topic, and it is smaller than you might fear.

Average velocity is x two minus x one over t two minus t one. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of delta x over delta t as delta t goes to zero, which is d x by d t. Two lines, and the second is what the first becomes when you squeeze the window shut.

Average acceleration is v two minus v one over t two minus t one. Instantaneous acceleration is d v by d t, equivalently d squared x by d t squared. Read that against the line above it and you should feel something clicking.

That something is the symmetry, and it is worth saying out loud. Every average is a difference over a difference — a change in the top quantity divided by the change in time it took. Every instantaneous value is that same ratio pushed to its limit. You are not learning four relations. You are learning one relation applied at two levels of the ladder, twice.
Now the two special-case averaging results, and these are the ones exams hunt with.

Equal distances at v one and v two: average speed is two v one v two over v one plus v two. That is the harmonic mean. Remember why from the last section — the slow leg hogs the clock, so the average gets dragged toward the slower speed.
Equal times at v one and v two: average speed is v one plus v two over two. The plain arithmetic mean. Each speed gets an equal slice of the clock, so neither can dominate.

<whisper>Now read the red note, because it is the most important sentence on this board. Memorise the distinction, not the formulas. Both results are two lines of first-principles work. What kills students is not forgetting the harmonic mean — it is grabbing the arithmetic one when the question said equal distances. Know which case you are in and the algebra is trivial.

And finally the two inequalities again, sitting in the formula sheet where they belong. Distance is greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement. Average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity. They are not decoration on the toolkit — they are the checks you run on everything the toolkit produces.
अब core relations, एक ही जगह इकट्ठी। यही इस sub-topic का आपका working toolkit है, और ये उतना बड़ा नहीं जितना डर लग रहा हो।

Average velocity है x two minus x one over t two minus t one. Instantaneous velocity है limit of delta x over delta t as delta t goes to zero, यानी d x by d t. दो lines, और दूसरी वही है जो पहली बन जाती है जब आप window बंद कर दें।
Average acceleration है v two minus v one over t two minus t one. Instantaneous acceleration है d v by d t, यानी d squared x by d t squared. इसे ऊपर वाली line के साथ पढ़िए और कुछ click होना चाहिए।

वो कुछ है symmetry, और इसे बोलकर कहना ज़रूरी है। हर average एक difference over a difference है — ऊपर वाली quantity का change बटा उतना time जो लगा। हर instantaneous value वही ratio है, limit तक धकेला हुआ। आप चार relations नहीं सीख रहे। आप एक ही relation सीख रहे हैं, सीढ़ी के दो levels पर, दो बार।
अब वो दो special-case averaging results, और exams इन्हीं के साथ शिकार करती हैं।

Equal distances at v one and v two: average speed है two v one v two over v one plus v two. यही harmonic mean है। पिछले section वाली वजह याद रखिए — slow leg घड़ी हड़प लेता है, तो average slower speed की तरफ़ खिंच जाता है।
Equal times at v one and v two: average speed है v one plus v two over two. सीधा arithmetic mean. हर speed को घड़ी का बराबर हिस्सा मिलता है, तो कोई हावी नहीं हो सकती।

<whisper>अब red note पढ़िए, क्योंकि इस board का यही सबसे ज़रूरी वाक्य है। Distinction याद रखिए, formulas नहीं। दोनों results first principles से दो lines का काम हैं। Students को harmonic mean भूलना नहीं मारता — उन्हें ये मारता है कि question में equal distances लिखा था और उन्होंने arithmetic वाला उठा लिया। कौन सा case है ये पता हो, तो algebra मामूली है।

और आख़िर में वही दो inequalities, formula sheet में अपनी सही जगह पर। Distance, displacement के magnitude से बड़ा या बराबर। Average speed, average velocity के magnitude से बड़ा या बराबर। ये toolkit की सजावट नहीं हैं — ये वो checks हैं जो आप toolkit की हर पैदावार पर चलाते हैं।

board_events.text: GIVEN: leg 1 = 300 m east in 100 s. Leg 2 = 100 m west in 50 s. Take east as positive.
(a) Total distance = magnitudes added = $300 + 100 = 400$ m.
Average speed $>$ $|$average velocity$|$ — exactly as the inequality promises, because he reversed.

segments.text: A board-level example, and it is the cleanest possible test of everything we just built. A jogger runs three hundred metres due east in one hundred seconds, then turns and runs one hundred metres due west in fifty seconds. Find the total distance, the displacement, the average speed, and the average velocity.

Look at the picture first, because the setup is the whole battle. Both legs are drawn on one number line, and east has been declared positive — that is step one of Procedure A, done before any arithmetic. The blue arrow is leg one running out to three hundred. The red arrow is leg two coming back to two hundred. He finishes at the two hundred metre mark.

So the given data, written with signs attached. Leg one is three hundred metres east in one hundred seconds. Leg two is one hundred metres west in fifty seconds. East is positive, so west is negative — and that convention is now locked for the rest of the problem.

Part a, total distance. Distance adds magnitudes and ignores direction entirely. Three hundred plus one hundred is four hundred metres. The jogger's legs did four hundred metres of work and they do not care that some of it pointed the other way.

Part b, displacement. Now the signs matter. Plus three hundred plus minus one hundred gives plus two hundred metres, which is two hundred metres east. Check it against the endpoints: he started at zero and finished at two hundred, so x final minus x initial is two hundred. The two methods agree, which is exactly the check Procedure A asks for.

Part c, average speed. Total time is one hundred plus fifty, which is one hundred fifty seconds. Average speed is total distance over total time — four hundred over one hundred fifty, roughly two point six seven metres per second. Note the numerator: distance, because this is speed.

Part d, average velocity. Same total time, but displacement on top. Two hundred over one hundred fifty, roughly one point three three metres per second, east. Same denominator, different numerator — and the direction comes along because velocity is a vector.

Now the red note, which is the real lesson. Average speed came out two point six seven; the magnitude of average velocity came out one point three three. Speed is bigger, exactly as the inequality promised — and it is bigger precisely because he reversed. Had he simply run four hundred metres east without turning, the two numbers would have been identical. The turn is what opened the gap.

एक board-level example, और ये हमने अभी जो बनाया उसका सबसे साफ़ test है। एक jogger three hundred metres due east दौड़ता है one hundred seconds में, फिर मुड़कर one hundred metres due west दौड़ता है fifty seconds में। Total distance, displacement, average speed, और average velocity निकालिए।

पहले picture देखिए, क्योंकि setup ही पूरी लड़ाई है। दोनों legs एक ही number line पर हैं, और east को positive घोषित किया गया है — यही Procedure A का step one, किसी भी arithmetic से पहले। Blue arrow leg one है, three hundred तक। Red arrow leg two है, two hundred पर वापस। वो two hundred metre mark पर ख़त्म करता है।

तो given data, signs के साथ। Leg one है three hundred metres east in one hundred seconds. Leg two है one hundred metres west in fifty seconds. East positive है, तो west negative — और ये convention अब पूरी problem के लिए lock है।

Part a, total distance. Distance magnitudes जोड़ता है और direction को बिलकुल नज़रअंदाज़ करता है। Three hundred plus one hundred, यानी four hundred metres. Jogger की टाँगों ने four hundred metres का काम किया, और उन्हें फ़र्क़ नहीं पड़ता कि कुछ हिस्सा उल्टी तरफ़ था।

Part b, displacement. अब signs मायने रखते हैं। Plus three hundred plus minus one hundred, यानी plus two hundred metres — two hundred metres east. Endpoints से check कीजिए: शुरू zero से, ख़त्म two hundred पर, तो x final minus x initial है two hundred. दोनों methods agree करते हैं, और Procedure A यही check माँगता है।

Part c, average speed. Total time है one hundred plus fifty, यानी one hundred fifty seconds. Average speed है total distance over total time — four hundred over one hundred fifty, लगभग two point six seven metres per second. Numerator ग़ौर कीजिए: distance, क्योंकि ये speed है।

Part d, average velocity. वही total time, मगर ऊपर displacement. Two hundred over one hundred fifty, लगभग one point three three metres per second, east. वही denominator, अलग numerator — और direction साथ आता है क्योंकि velocity vector है।

अब red note, जो असली सबक़ है। Average speed आया two point six seven; average velocity का magnitude आया one point three three. Speed बड़ा है, बिलकुल जैसा inequality ने वादा किया था — और बड़ा इसीलिए है क्योंकि वो मुड़ा। अगर वो सीधा four hundred metres east दौड़ता बिना मुड़े, तो दोनों numbers एक जैसे आते। Gap उसी मोड़ ने खोला।

board_events.text: OPTIONS: (A) 50 km/h  (B) 48 km/h  (C) 52 km/h  (D) 24 km/h
THE TRAP: the eye jumps to $(40+60)/2 = 50$, option (A). But the arithmetic mean is WRONG for equal distances.
'Second half (equal distance)' — those two words decide the entire question.
ANSWER: (B) 48 km/h.
SPEED CUE: the harmonic mean is ALWAYS less than the arithmetic mean. See 'equal distances, two speeds' and eliminate the simple average — pick the slightly smaller value. You barely need to compute.

segments.text: Now a N E E T speed trap, and this one is worth real attention because it is a fast M C Q that the source calls the single most-tested trap in this sub-topic. A bus covers the first half of a route at forty kilometres per hour, and the second half — equal distance — at sixty. Its average speed for the whole route is what?
The picture lays the trap bare. Two equal stretches, same length d each, one at forty and one at sixty. Look at the red box and the green box side by side; that is the entire question in one image.
The options are fifty, forty eight, fifty two, and twenty four. And I want you to notice something before we compute: fifty is sitting there first, and it is the answer your eye wants.

Here is why, in the red note. The eye sees forty and sixty and jumps straight to their simple average, forty plus sixty over two, which is fifty. Option A. It feels obviously right. And it is wrong — because the arithmetic mean is only correct for equal times, and this question gave equal distances.

Go back and read the question. Second half, equal distance. Those two words decide the entire problem. They are not scenery, they are the question. This is why Procedure B opens with 'which pieces are equal?' — everything else is downstream of that.

So, equal distances means harmonic mean. Two v one v two over v one plus v two. That is two times forty times sixty, over forty plus sixty. The top is four thousand eight hundred, the bottom is one hundred. Forty eight kilometres per hour.

Answer is B, forty eight. And sanity-check it against what we said earlier: the average must lie between forty and sixty — it does. And for equal distances it must sit closer to the slower speed — forty eight is nearer forty than sixty. Both checks pass. Fifty would have failed the second one.

<whisper>Now the speed cue, and this is what actually wins you the mark under time pressure. The harmonic mean is always less than the arithmetic mean. Always. So the instant you see 'equal distances, two speeds', cross out the simple average and pick the slightly smaller value. In this question that is enough to land on forty eight without computing anything at all.

अब एक N E E T speed trap, और ये सच में ध्यान देने लायक़ है क्योंकि ये तेज़ M C Q है जिसे source इस sub-topic का सबसे ज़्यादा test होने वाला trap कहता है। एक bus route का पहला half चलती है forty kilometres per hour पर, और दूसरा half — equal distance — sixty पर। पूरे route की average speed क्या है?
Picture trap को खोलकर रख देती है। दो बराबर stretches, दोनों की length वही d, एक forty पर एक sixty पर। Red box और green box साथ-साथ देखिए; पूरा सवाल इसी एक image में है।
Options हैं fifty, forty eight, fifty two, और twenty four. और compute करने से पहले एक चीज़ notice कीजिए: fifty सबसे पहले बैठा है, और यही वो answer है जो आपकी आँख चाहती है।

वजह red note में है। आँख forty और sixty देखकर सीधे उनके simple average पर कूदती है, forty plus sixty over two, यानी fifty. Option A. लगता बिलकुल सही है। और है ग़लत — क्योंकि arithmetic mean सिर्फ़ equal times के लिए सही है, और इस question में equal distances दी हैं।

वापस जाकर question पढ़िए। Second half, equal distance. यही दो शब्द पूरी problem तय कर देते हैं। ये सजावट नहीं हैं, यही सवाल हैं। इसीलिए Procedure B शुरू ही होता है इससे कि कौन से टुकड़े बराबर हैं — बाक़ी सब उसी के बाद आता है।

तो equal distances का मतलब harmonic mean. Two v one v two over v one plus v two. यानी two into forty into sixty, बटा forty plus sixty. ऊपर आया four thousand eight hundred, नीचे one hundred. Forty eight kilometres per hour.

Answer है B, forty eight. और जो हमने पहले कहा उससे sanity-check कीजिए: average forty और sixty के बीच होना चाहिए — है। और equal distances में slower speed के क़रीब होना चाहिए — forty eight, sixty के मुक़ाबले forty के ज़्यादा पास है। दोनों checks pass. Fifty दूसरा check fail कर देता।

<whisper>अब speed cue, और time pressure में असल में यही आपको mark दिलाता है। Harmonic mean हमेशा arithmetic mean से कम होता है। हमेशा। तो जिस पल 'equal distances, two speeds' दिखे, simple average काट दीजिए और थोड़ी छोटी value उठा लीजिए। इस question में इतना ही काफ़ी है forty eight तक पहुँचने के लिए, बिना कुछ compute किए।

sections.title: Example 3 [JEE Main]: differentiate, then find distance vs displacement

board_events.text: $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + 5$ (metres, $t$ in seconds)
WHY IT'S MULTI-CONCEPT: it fuses differentiation with the distance-vs-displacement distinction.
(a) At rest means $v = 0$, so $t = 1$ s and $t = 3$ s.
The negative sign means it is moving in the $-x$ direction at that instant — NOT that it is decelerating.

segments.text: A J E E Main level example now, and it is a favourite because it fuses two things that sit in different corners of your brain — calculus, and the distance-versus-displacement distinction. A particle on the x-axis has position x of t equals t cubed minus six t squared plus nine t plus five, in metres.

That is why it is multi-concept, and why it catches people. Students who can differentiate cleanly then forget to think about reversals; students who understand reversals fumble the factorisation. You need both, in the same three minutes.

Start by going down the ladder. Differentiate position and you get velocity: three t squared minus twelve t plus nine. And now do the single most useful thing available — factorise it. Three times t minus one, times t minus three. Differentiate once more for acceleration: six t minus twelve. Two derivatives, and the whole problem is now open.

Part a asks when it is momentarily at rest. At rest means v equals zero, and the factorised form hands it to you instantly: t equals one second and t equals three seconds. That factorisation just saved you a quadratic formula, which is exactly why you do it before you need it.

Part b. Acceleration zero means six t minus twelve equals zero, so t equals two seconds. Now substitute back into velocity: v of two is three times one, times minus one, which is minus three metres per second.

Read the red note carefully, because this is where marks leak. The negative sign does not mean the particle is decelerating. It means the particle is moving in the minus x direction at that instant. Sign of velocity is direction of motion, full stop. Deceleration is about velocity and acceleration pointing opposite ways, which is a different statement entirely.

Part c, and now look at the picture, because it is the whole answer. Compute the positions: x of zero is five, x of one is nine, x of three is five. From t equals zero to one the velocity is positive — the blue arrow — and it moves forward four metres. From t equals one to three the velocity is negative — the red arrow — and it comes back four metres.
So the two boxes. Displacement is x of three minus x of zero, which is five minus five, zero. Distance is the magnitude of plus four plus the magnitude of minus four, which is eight metres.

Sit with that for a second. The particle ends exactly where it started — zero displacement — and yet it covered eight metres of path. And the culprit is visible on the board: the reversal at t equals one second. Without that turn the two numbers would be identical. With it, they disagree by the full width of the round trip. This is the jogger and the cricketer again, wearing a cubic.

अब एक J E E Main level example, और ये favourite है क्योंकि ये दो ऐसी चीज़ें जोड़ता है जो दिमाग़ के अलग कोनों में बैठी हैं — calculus, और distance-versus-displacement distinction. X-axis पर एक particle की position है x of t equals t cubed minus six t squared plus nine t plus five, metres में।

इसीलिए ये multi-concept है, और इसीलिए ये लोगों को पकड़ता है। जो साफ़ differentiate कर लेते हैं वो reversals सोचना भूल जाते हैं; जो reversals समझते हैं वो factorisation में लड़खड़ाते हैं। दोनों चाहिए, उन्हीं तीन minutes में।

सीढ़ी से नीचे उतरकर शुरू कीजिए। Position को differentiate कीजिए, velocity मिलती है: three t squared minus twelve t plus nine. और अब सबसे काम की चीज़ कीजिए — factorise. Three into t minus one, into t minus three. Acceleration के लिए एक बार और differentiate: six t minus twelve. दो derivatives, और पूरी problem अब खुली पड़ी है।

Part a पूछता है कब वो momentarily at rest है। At rest यानी v equals zero, और factorised form तुरंत दे देता है: t equals one second और t equals three seconds. उस factorisation ने अभी आपका quadratic formula बचा दिया — इसीलिए ज़रूरत पड़ने से पहले कर लेते हैं।
Part b. Acceleration zero यानी six t minus twelve equals zero, तो t equals two seconds. अब velocity में वापस डालिए: v of two है three into one, into minus one, यानी minus three metres per second.

Red note ध्यान से पढ़िए, यहीं marks रिसते हैं। वो negative sign ये नहीं कहता कि particle decelerate हो रहा है। वो कहता है कि particle उस instant पर minus x direction में चल रहा है। Velocity का sign motion का direction है, बस। Deceleration का मतलब है velocity और acceleration का उल्टी तरफ़ होना — वो बिलकुल अलग बात है।

Part c, और अब picture देखिए, क्योंकि पूरा answer वही है। Positions निकालिए: x of zero है five, x of one है nine, x of three है five. T equals zero से one तक velocity positive है — blue arrow — और वो चार metres आगे जाता है। T equals one से three तक velocity negative है — red arrow — और वो चार metres वापस आता है।
तो दोनों boxes. Displacement है x of three minus x of zero, यानी five minus five, zero. Distance है magnitude of plus four plus magnitude of minus four, यानी eight metres.

एक पल इसके साथ बैठिए। Particle बिलकुल वहीं ख़त्म करता है जहाँ से शुरू किया — displacement zero — और फिर भी उसने eight metres का path तय किया। और मुजरिम board पर दिख रहा है: t equals one second पर reversal. उस मोड़ के बिना दोनों numbers एक जैसे होते। उसके साथ, वो पूरे round trip जितना अलग हो जाते हैं। यही jogger और cricketer हैं, cubic पहनकर।

segments.text: J E E Advanced level, and this is the sub-topic's final boss. A particle moves along a straight line with velocity v of t equals t squared minus six t plus eight, over zero to five seconds. Find the instants it reverses, the total displacement, the total distance, and both averages — and verify the inequality holds.

The reasoning first, because if you get this framing right the algebra is routine. Direction reverses wherever v changes sign. Displacement is the plain integral of v d t — signs and all, let the negatives cancel. But distance needs the integral of the modulus of v, done piecewise, because distance must never be allowed to cancel. That is the whole difference: one integral lets backtracking subtract, the other does not.

Look at the picture and the structure appears. The parabola dips below the axis between two and four. Blue regions are forward motion, the red region between them is backtracking. Three pieces, and you must handle them separately or the physics quietly lies to you.

So factorise. V equals t minus two, times t minus four. Zero at t equals two and t equals four seconds. Test the sign in each stretch: positive on zero to two, negative on two to four, positive on four to five. That is part a — two reversals, at t equals two and t equals four seconds, exactly where the curve crosses.

Now take an antiderivative once and reuse it everywhere. F of t equals t cubed over three, minus three t squared, plus eight t. Evaluate it at the four moments that matter: F of zero is zero, F of two is twenty over three, F of four is sixteen over three, F of five is twenty over three. Four numbers, and every remaining part of the question is built from them.

Part b, displacement. Plain integral from zero to five, which is F of five minus F of zero — twenty over three, about six point six seven metres. Notice we did not care about the roots at all here. Displacement is endpoints only, just as it always was.

Part c, distance. Now the roots matter enormously. Take each piece and add its magnitude: twenty over three from the first, then the magnitude of sixteen over three minus twenty over three, which is four over three, then four over three again from the last piece. Total twenty eight over three, about nine point three three metres. This is the pro-tip in action — split at the roots before integrating, or the backtracking silently cancels and you report distance when you have computed displacement.

Part d. Over five seconds total: average velocity is twenty over three, over five, about one point three three metres per second. Average speed is twenty eight over three, over five, about one point eight seven.

And the red note closes the loop beautifully. One point eight seven is indeed greater than one point three three — the inequality holds, as it must. But look closer at where the gap came from. It is exactly the wasted backtracking between t equals two and t equals four. The particle spent that stretch undoing its own progress; distance counted it, displacement cancelled it, and the difference between the two averages is precisely the price of that detour.

J E E Advanced level, और ये इस sub-topic का final boss है। एक particle straight line पर चलता है velocity v of t equals t squared minus six t plus eight के साथ, zero से five seconds तक। कब reverse होता है, total displacement, total distance, और दोनों averages निकालिए — और verify कीजिए कि inequality क़ायम है।

पहले reasoning, क्योंकि framing सही हो गई तो algebra routine है। Direction वहीं reverse होता है जहाँ v का sign बदले। Displacement है plain integral of v d t — signs समेत, negatives को cancel होने दीजिए। मगर distance के लिए चाहिए modulus of v का integral, piecewise, क्योंकि distance को cancel होने की इजाज़त कभी नहीं। पूरा फ़र्क़ यही है: एक integral backtracking को घटाने देता है, दूसरा नहीं।

Picture देखिए और structure सामने आ जाता है। Parabola two और four के बीच axis के नीचे डुबकी लगाती है। Blue regions forward motion हैं, बीच का red region backtracking है। तीन टुकड़े, और इन्हें अलग-अलग संभालना ही होगा वरना physics चुपचाप झूठ बोल देगी।

तो factorise कीजिए। V equals t minus two, into t minus four. Zero at t equals two और t equals four seconds. हर stretch में sign test कीजिए: zero से two पर positive, two से four पर negative, four से five पर positive. यही part a है — दो reversals, t equals two और t equals four seconds पर, ठीक वहीं जहाँ curve crossing करती है।

अब antiderivative एक बार निकालिए और हर जगह इस्तेमाल कीजिए। F of t equals t cubed over three, minus three t squared, plus eight t. उन चार moments पर evaluate कीजिए जो मायने रखते हैं: F of zero है zero, F of two है twenty over three, F of four है sixteen over three, F of five है twenty over three. चार numbers, और question का बाक़ी हर हिस्सा इन्हीं से बनेगा।

Part b, displacement. Plain integral zero से five, यानी F of five minus F of zero — twenty over three, लगभग six point six seven metres. ग़ौर कीजिए यहाँ roots की परवाह ही नहीं की। Displacement सिर्फ़ endpoints है, जैसा हमेशा से था।

Part c, distance. अब roots बेहद मायने रखते हैं। हर टुकड़ा लीजिए और उसका magnitude जोड़िए: पहले से twenty over three, फिर sixteen over three minus twenty over three का magnitude, यानी four over three, फिर आख़िरी टुकड़े से फिर four over three. Total twenty eight over three, लगभग nine point three three metres. यही pro-tip काम करते हुए — integrate करने से पहले roots पर तोड़िए, वरना backtracking चुपचाप cancel हो जाएगा और आप displacement निकालकर उसे distance बता देंगे।

Part d. कुल five seconds पर: average velocity है twenty over three, बटा five, लगभग one point three three metres per second. Average speed है twenty eight over three, बटा five, लगभग one point eight seven.

और red note loop को ख़ूबसूरती से बंद करता है। One point eight seven सच में one point three three से बड़ा है — inequality क़ायम है, जैसा होना ही था। मगर ग़ौर से देखिए ये gap आया कहाँ से। ये बिलकुल वही बर्बाद हुआ backtracking है t equals two से four के बीच। Particle ने वो stretch अपनी ही तरक़्क़ी उलटने में लगाया; distance ने उसे गिना, displacement ने उसे cancel किया, और दोनों averages का फ़र्क़ ठीक उसी चक्कर की क़ीमत है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: kinematic quantities

board_events.text: Four traps that cost marks every year
1. Treating distance and displacement as interchangeable. They coincide ONLY for straight, one-way motion. Always ask: did the body turn around?
2. Arithmetic-averaging speeds over equal DISTANCES. Two equal stretches at 40 and 60 is not 50 — it is the harmonic mean, 48. Arithmetic mean is correct only for equal TIMES.
3. Assuming $v = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$. At a turning point the body is instantaneously at rest yet still accelerating. Velocity and acceleration are independent at an instant.
4. Forgetting to fix a positive direction in 1-D. Without a sign convention, '$-3$ m/s' is meaningless and sign errors cascade.
PRO-TIP: lock in one phrase — 'same distance $\to$ harmonic, same time $\to$ arithmetic.'
For average velocity, NEVER integrate the wiggly path. It is simply $(x_{final} - x_{initial}) \,/\, \text{total time}$ — endpoints only.
When a velocity function changes sign, SPLIT the time axis at the roots before integrating for distance — or you will silently cancel the back-tracking and report distance as displacement.

segments.text: Let us close this sub-topic by naming the traps, because these four cost marks every single year, and every one of them is avoidable with a single question asked at the right moment.

Trap one: treating distance and displacement as interchangeable. They coincide only for straight, one-way motion. The moment the direction reverses — or the path curves — distance pulls ahead and stays ahead. So build the habit of asking one question of every problem: did the body turn around? If yes, those two numbers are different, and any step that assumes otherwise is already wrong.

Trap two, the expensive one: arithmetic-averaging speeds over equal distances. Two equal stretches at forty and sixty is not fifty. It is the harmonic mean, forty eight. The arithmetic mean is correct only for equal times. This trap works because fifty is genuinely the first number your brain produces, and because the wrong answer is always sitting in the options waiting for you.

Trap three: assuming zero velocity forces zero acceleration. At a turning point the body is instantaneously at rest, and still accelerating at full strength — the top of a vertical throw is the standard picture, but it is true of any reversal. Velocity and acceleration are independent at an instant. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other.

Trap four, the quiet one: forgetting to fix a positive direction. Without a sign convention, minus three metres per second is not a wrong value, it is a meaningless one — minus three relative to what? And the damage is not local. One unfixed convention and sign errors cascade through every line that follows.

Now the pro-tips. First, lock in one phrase and let it do the work: same distance goes to harmonic, same time goes to arithmetic. Say it in that rhythm until it is automatic. Under exam pressure you will not have time to re-derive it — but you will have time to recall a phrase.

Second, and this one saves real minutes: for average velocity, never integrate the wiggly path. Average velocity is x final minus x initial, over total time. Endpoints only. Students see a complicated position function and start setting up integrals when a subtraction was all that was required. Displacement never cared about the middle of the journey, and neither does average velocity.

<whisper>And the last one, which is the difference between a good student and a careless one. When a velocity function changes sign, split the time axis at the roots before you integrate for distance. Skip that split and the integral will silently cancel your backtracking against your forward motion — and you will confidently report a displacement while calling it a distance. It will not look like an error. That is exactly what makes it dangerous.
इस sub-topic को traps के नाम लेकर बंद करते हैं, क्योंकि ये चारों हर साल marks खाते हैं, और हर एक से बचा जा सकता है — बस सही वक़्त पर एक सवाल पूछकर।

Trap one: distance और displacement को एक जैसा समझना। ये सिर्फ़ straight, one-way motion में मिलते हैं। जिस पल direction reverse हुआ — या path मुड़ा — distance आगे निकल जाता है और आगे ही रहता है। तो हर problem से एक सवाल पूछने की आदत बनाइए: क्या body मुड़ी थी? अगर हाँ, तो वो दोनों numbers अलग हैं, और जो भी step उल्टा मानकर चला वो पहले ही ग़लत है।

Trap two, महँगा वाला: equal distances पर speeds का arithmetic average निकालना। Forty और sixty पर दो बराबर stretches का जवाब fifty नहीं है। वो harmonic mean है, forty eight. Arithmetic mean सिर्फ़ equal times के लिए सही है। ये trap इसलिए चलता है क्योंकि आपका दिमाग़ सबसे पहले सच में fifty ही बनाता है, और ग़लत answer हमेशा options में आपका इंतज़ार करता बैठा होता है।

Trap three: ये मान लेना कि zero velocity से acceleration भी zero हो जाएगा। Turning point पर body instantaneously at rest होती है, और पूरी ताक़त से accelerate भी हो रही होती है — vertical throw का top standard picture है, मगर ये किसी भी reversal पर सच है। Instant पर velocity और acceleration independent हैं। एक को जानकर दूसरे का कुछ पता नहीं चलता।

Trap four, चुपचाप वाला: positive direction fix करना भूल जाना। Sign convention के बिना minus three metres per second ग़लत value नहीं है, वो बेमानी value है — minus three किसके सापेक्ष? और नुक़सान वहीं नहीं रुकता। एक unfixed convention, और sign errors हर आने वाली line में फैल जाते हैं।

अब pro-tips. पहला, एक phrase lock कीजिए और उसे काम करने दीजिए: same distance goes to harmonic, same time goes to arithmetic. इसी लय में दोहराइए जब तक ये अपने आप न आ जाए। Exam pressure में दोबारा derive करने का वक़्त नहीं होगा — मगर एक phrase याद करने का वक़्त होगा।

दूसरा, और ये सच में minutes बचाता है: average velocity के लिए उस टेढ़े path को कभी integrate मत कीजिए। Average velocity है x final minus x initial, बटा total time. सिर्फ़ endpoints. Students एक पेचीदा position function देखकर integrals लगाने लगते हैं जबकि सिर्फ़ एक subtraction चाहिए था। Displacement को journey के बीच से कभी मतलब नहीं था, average velocity को भी नहीं है।

<whisper>और आख़िरी वाला, जो अच्छे student और लापरवाह student का फ़र्क़ है। जब velocity function का sign बदले, तो distance के लिए integrate करने से पहले time axis को roots पर तोड़िए। ये तोड़ना छोड़ दिया, तो integral चुपचाप आपके backtracking को forward motion के ख़िलाफ़ cancel कर देगा — और आप पूरे यक़ीन से displacement बताएँगे और उसे distance कहेंगे। ये error जैसा दिखेगा ही नहीं। यही इसे ख़तरनाक बनाता है।
