board_events.text: By SYMMETRY it returns to the launch point with the SAME speed it left with.
Equal time up and down. The flight time is exactly twice the time to the top.
At the very top its velocity is momentarily ZERO, but its acceleration is still a full $g$ downward. Gravity never switches off.
The ball does not hang weightless at the top — it is about to fall.

segments.text: Before we derive anything, there is a consequence of free fall worth feeling in your bones, because once you have it, a whole class of questions becomes almost free.

Picture a ball thrown straight up. It rises, it slows, it stops for one instant at the top, and it falls back. That much you know from having thrown things. The physics adds something surprising to it.

Look at the diagram. The blue arrow on the left is the ball leaving your hand with speed u. The red arrow on the right is it returning. And the green brackets underneath are the two halves of the flight.

Here is the surprise, or rather the elegance. By symmetry it returns to the launch point with exactly the same speed it left with. Not roughly. Exactly. Throw it up at twenty metres per second and it comes back into your hand at twenty metres per second. It is the same physics running backwards — gravity took speed away on the way up at exactly the rate it gives speed back on the way down.
So the results on the board fall out. Maximum height above the launch point is u squared over two g. Time to the top is u over g. And total flight time back to the start is two u over g.

Look at that last one and notice what it is saying. The time up equals the time down — the green brackets in the picture are the same width. So the flight time is exactly twice the time to the top. That means you almost never have to compute the descent separately. Solve the way up and double it.

Now the red note, which is the trap sitting inside all this elegance. At the very top the ball's velocity is momentarily zero. Every student sees that. What they then assume is that the acceleration is zero too — and it is not. It is still a full g downward, at that exact instant, unchanged.

So the ball does not hang weightless at the top, however much it looks like it does. It is about to fall, and it is being accelerated the whole time it appears to pause. This is the zero-velocity trap from Sub-topic one, and free fall is where the exam most loves to set it.
कुछ भी derive करने से पहले, free fall का एक नतीजा है जिसे हड्डियों में महसूस करना चाहिए, क्योंकि ये आ गया तो सवालों की एक पूरी क़िस्म लगभग मुफ़्त हो जाती है।

एक ball की कल्पना कीजिए जो सीधा ऊपर फेंकी गई। वो उठती है, धीमी होती है, ऊपर एक instant के लिए रुकती है, और वापस गिरती है। इतना तो आप चीज़ें फेंककर जानते ही हैं। Physics इसमें कुछ हैरान करने वाला जोड़ती है।
Diagram देखिए। बाईं तरफ़ blue arrow वो ball है जो आपके हाथ से speed u के साथ निकलती है। दाईं तरफ़ red arrow वो वापस आती हुई है। और नीचे green brackets flight के दो हिस्से हैं।

हैरानी — या कहिए ख़ूबसूरती — ये है। Symmetry से वो launch point पर बिलकुल उसी speed के साथ लौटती है जिससे गई थी। लगभग नहीं। बिलकुल। Twenty metres per second से ऊपर फेंकिए और वो आपके हाथ में twenty metres per second से वापस आएगी। ये वही physics है उल्टी चलती हुई — gravity ने ऊपर जाते वक़्त ठीक उसी rate से speed छीनी जिस rate से नीचे आते वक़्त वापस देती है।
तो board वाले results अपने आप निकल आते हैं। Launch point से maximum height है u squared over two g. ऊपर तक का time है u over g. और वापस शुरुआत तक का total flight time है two u over g.

आख़िरी वाला देखिए और ग़ौर कीजिए ये क्या कह रहा है। Time up बराबर time down — picture में दोनों green brackets की चौड़ाई एक है। तो flight time ऊपर तक के time का ठीक दुगना है। मतलब आपको descent अलग से लगभग कभी compute नहीं करना पड़ेगा। ऊपर वाला हिस्सा solve कीजिए और दुगना कर दीजिए।

अब red note, जो इस पूरी ख़ूबसूरती के अंदर बैठा trap है। बिलकुल ऊपर ball की velocity एक पल के लिए zero होती है। ये हर student देख लेता है। फिर वो मान लेता है कि acceleration भी zero होगा — और वो नहीं है। वो उसी exact instant पर पूरा g downward है, बिना बदले।

तो ball ऊपर weightless लटकती नहीं, चाहे वो कितना ही ऐसा दिखे। वो गिरने ही वाली है, और जितनी देर वो ठहरी दिखती है उतनी देर भी accelerate हो रही है। ये Sub-topic one वाला zero-velocity trap है, और free fall वो जगह है जहाँ exam इसे सबसे ज़्यादा बिछाना पसंद करती है।

board_events.text: You must fix a positive direction FIRST. Then sign EVERY quantity — $u$, $a$ and $s$ — to match it.
UP $=$ POSITIVE: then $a = -g$. A ball thrown up has $u > 0$; ground below the launch point is $s < 0$.
DOWN $=$ POSITIVE: then $a = +g$. Convenient for a simple drop, where everything comes out positive.
Both are correct. What wrecks vertical-motion problems is MIXING them mid-solution.
Free fall also assumes: no air resistance, $g$ effectively constant (valid near the surface), and the body treated as a POINT MASS.
PRO-TIP: lock in 'up $=$ positive, $a = -g$' for every vertical problem and never re-decide.

segments.text: Before we derive the equations, one more piece of housekeeping — and I promise it is the highest-return thirty seconds in this sub-topic. The source is blunt: a sign slip on u, a, or s is the most common source of wrong answers here.

Look at the two panels. On the left, up is positive. On the right, down is positive. Both are drawn correctly. Both will get you the right answer. Neither is more true than the other — a sign convention is a choice you make, not a fact you discover.

So the rule is: fix a positive direction first, and then sign every quantity to match it. Not just the ones that feel directional. Initial velocity, acceleration, and displacement all get signed by the same convention, together, before you write a single equation.

Take the left panel. Up is positive, so gravity — which points down — becomes a equals minus g. A ball thrown up has u positive. And if the ball ends up below where it started, its displacement s is negative. Notice that minus sign on s is not an error creeping in; it is the convention doing its job, telling you the ball finished below the origin.

The right panel is the other choice. Down is positive, so a equals plus g. For a body simply dropped, u is zero and everything else comes out positive — no minus signs anywhere in the working. That is genuinely convenient for straightforward drops, and it is why you will see it used for them.

The red note is the whole point. Both conventions are correct. What wrecks vertical-motion problems is mixing them mid-solution — deciding up is positive, writing a as minus ten, then halfway down the page treating a downward displacement as positive because it 'feels' like a distance. The convention does not care about your feelings. Apply it to every quantity or to none.

While we are collecting conditions, here are the rest of free fall's fine print. No air resistance. G effectively constant, which is valid near the surface but would fail if you went high enough. And the body treated as a point mass — no spinning, no shape, no size. Every free-fall answer you produce carries those three assumptions.

<whisper>And the pro-tip that saves you from the whole mess: lock in up equals positive, a equals minus g, for every vertical problem. Every one. Do not optimise per question. The five seconds you save by picking the convenient convention are not worth the risk of re-deciding under pressure and contradicting yourself three lines later.

Equations derive करने से पहले एक और घरेलू काम — और यक़ीन कीजिए, इस sub-topic के ये सबसे ज़्यादा फ़ायदे वाले तीस seconds हैं। Source बेलाग कहता है: u, a, या s पर sign का फिसलना यहाँ ग़लत answers की सबसे आम वजह है।

दोनों panels देखिए। बाएँ, up positive है। दाएँ, down positive है। दोनों सही खींचे गए हैं। दोनों से सही answer आएगा। कोई दूसरे से ज़्यादा सच्चा नहीं — sign convention एक चुनाव है जो आप करते हैं, कोई खोजा हुआ fact नहीं।

तो rule ये है: पहले positive direction fix कीजिए, फिर हर quantity को उसी के हिसाब से sign दीजिए। सिर्फ़ उन्हें नहीं जो directional महसूस होती हैं। Initial velocity, acceleration, और displacement — तीनों को एक ही convention से, एक साथ, एक भी equation लिखने से पहले।

बायाँ panel लीजिए। Up positive है, तो gravity — जो नीचे है — बन जाती है a equals minus g. ऊपर फेंकी ball का u positive है। और अगर ball वहाँ से नीचे ख़त्म करे जहाँ से शुरू किया था, तो उसका displacement s negative है। ग़ौर कीजिए s पर वो minus sign कोई घुसती हुई ग़लती नहीं है; वो convention अपना काम कर रही है, आपको बता रही है कि ball origin के नीचे ख़त्म हुई।

दायाँ panel दूसरा चुनाव है। Down positive है, तो a equals plus g. सिर्फ़ गिराई गई body के लिए u zero है और बाक़ी सब positive आता है — पूरी working में कहीं minus नहीं। सीधे-सादे drops के लिए ये सच में सुविधाजनक है, और इसीलिए वहाँ ये इस्तेमाल होता दिखेगा।

Red note ही असली बात है। दोनों conventions सही हैं। Vertical-motion problems को बर्बाद करता है इन्हें बीच solution में मिलाना — तय करना कि up positive है, a को minus ten लिखना, और फिर आधे page नीचे एक downward displacement को positive मान लेना क्योंकि वो 'distance जैसा लगता है'। Convention को आपकी feelings से मतलब नहीं। या तो हर quantity पर लगाइए, या किसी पर नहीं।

और चलते-चलते free fall की बाक़ी बारीक शर्तें भी नोट कर लीजिए। कोई air resistance नहीं। G effectively constant, जो surface के पास सही है मगर काफ़ी ऊपर जाने पर टूट जाएगा। और body को point mass माना गया — कोई घुमाव नहीं, कोई shape नहीं, कोई size नहीं। आपका हर free-fall answer इन तीन assumptions को साथ लेकर चलता है।

<whisper>और वो pro-tip जो आपको इस पूरे झमेले से बचाता है: हर vertical problem के लिए lock कीजिए — up equals positive, a equals minus g. हर एक के लिए। हर question पर optimise मत कीजिए। सुविधाजनक convention चुनकर बचाए गए पाँच seconds उस ख़तरे के लायक़ नहीं हैं कि आप दबाव में दोबारा फ़ैसला करें और तीन lines बाद ख़ुद का ही खंडन कर दें।

sections.subtopic: Equations of Motion and Free Fall
sections.title: Derivation 1: $v = u + at$, from the definition of acceleration

board_events.text: CBSE Board derivation — 2-3 marks, asked regularly
SETUP: a body with constant acceleration $a$ and initial velocity $u$; after time $t$ its velocity is $v$, having covered displacement $s$.
Constant acceleration means $a = dv/dt$ is FIXED. Rearrange and integrate from the start ($v = u$ at $t = 0$) to time $t$.
WHY THIS STEP: acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If that rate is constant, velocity grows LINEARLY with time.
The body gains exactly $a$ each second — so after $t$ seconds it has gained $at$, on top of whatever $u$ it started with.

segments.text: The board asks you to derive one of these three equations for two or three marks, regularly. So let us do all three properly. And notice these are derivations, not tricks — each one comes from a definition you already have.

Set the stage first, and keep this setup for all three. A body moves with constant acceleration a. Its initial velocity is u. After time t its velocity is v, and it has covered displacement s. Five quantities, and each derivation connects a different subset of them.

Derivation one starts from the definition of acceleration itself. Constant acceleration means a equals d v by d t, and that a is fixed — it is a number, not a function. So rearrange: d v equals a d t. Now integrate both sides from the start of the motion to time t. On the left, velocity runs from u to v. On the right, time runs from zero to t.
That is the line on the board: the integral of d v from u to v, equals the integral of a d t from zero to t.

Evaluate it. The left side is simply v minus u. The right side — and this is where constant a earns its keep — a is a constant, so it comes straight out of the integral, leaving a times the integral of d t from zero to t, which is a t. So v minus u equals a t. Had a been a function of time, that step would have been illegal, and this is exactly where the derivation would have collapsed.
Rearrange and you have it: v equals u plus a t. Our first equation of motion, and it took two lines.

The red note is what an examiner wants to see alongside the algebra — the reason. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If that rate is constant, then velocity grows linearly with time. Linear growth is exactly what v equals u plus a t describes: a straight line, with u as the intercept and a as the slope. That is why the v-t graph of uniform acceleration is a straight line — the same fact seen from Sub-topic two.

And here is the sentence to carry: the body gains exactly a of velocity every second. So after t seconds it has gained a t. Add that onto whatever u it started with, and you have v. Read that way, the equation is not something to memorise. It is bookkeeping.

Board इन तीन में से किसी एक equation की derivation दो या तीन marks के लिए नियमित रूप से पूछता है। तो चलिए तीनों ठीक से करते हैं। और ग़ौर कीजिए ये derivations हैं, tricks नहीं — हर एक उसी definition से निकलती है जो आपके पास पहले से है।

पहले मंच तैयार कीजिए, और यही setup तीनों के लिए रखिए। एक body constant acceleration a से चल रही है। इसकी initial velocity u है। Time t के बाद इसकी velocity v है, और इसने displacement s तय किया है। पाँच quantities, और हर derivation इनके अलग-अलग subset को जोड़ती है।

Derivation one ख़ुद acceleration की definition से शुरू होती है। Constant acceleration का मतलब a equals d v by d t, और वो a fixed है — वो एक number है, function नहीं। तो rearrange कीजिए: d v equals a d t. अब दोनों तरफ़ integrate कीजिए, motion की शुरुआत से time t तक। बाईं तरफ़ velocity u से v तक जाती है। दाईं तरफ़ time zero से t तक।
यही board वाली line है: integral of d v from u to v, equals integral of a d t from zero to t.

Evaluate कीजिए। बायाँ हिस्सा सीधा v minus u है। दायाँ हिस्सा — और यहीं constant a अपनी क़ीमत वसूल करता है — a एक constant है, तो वो सीधा integral से बाहर आ जाता है, और बचता है a into integral of d t from zero to t, यानी a t. तो v minus u equals a t. अगर a time का function होता, तो वो step नाजायज़ होता, और derivation ठीक वहीं ढह जाती।
Rearrange कीजिए और मिल गया: v equals u plus a t. हमारी पहली equation of motion, और दो lines में।

Red note वो है जो examiner algebra के साथ देखना चाहता है — वजह। Acceleration velocity का rate of change है। अगर वो rate constant है, तो velocity time के साथ linearly बढ़ती है। Linear growth बिलकुल वही है जो v equals u plus a t बताता है: एक straight line, u intercept और a slope. इसीलिए uniform acceleration का v-t graph straight line होता है — वही fact, Sub-topic two से देखा हुआ।

और ये वाक्य साथ ले जाइए: body हर second बिलकुल a जितनी velocity कमाती है। तो t seconds बाद उसने a t कमाया। जो u लेकर चली थी उस पर ये जोड़ दीजिए, और v मिल गया। ऐसे पढ़िए तो ये equation रटने की चीज़ नहीं है। ये हिसाब-किताब है।

sections.title: Derivation 2: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, from the area under $v$-$t$

board_events.text: A rectangle sitting under a triangle
Since velocity rises LINEARLY from $u$ to $v$, the $v$-$t$ graph is a straight line — and displacement is the AREA beneath it.

board_events.text: Now substitute $v - u = at$ from equation (1).
WHY THIS STEP: the RECTANGLE is the distance the body would cover at its starting speed; the TRIANGLE is the EXTRA that the speeding-up contributes.
This derivation is Sub-topic 2's 'area under $v$-$t$ is displacement' doing real work.

segments.text: Derivation two, and it is my favourite because it does not need any new machinery at all. It just cashes in what you already learned about graphs.

Here is the observation that starts it. We just proved velocity rises linearly from u to v. Linear means the v-t graph is a straight line. And from Sub-topic two we know the area under a v-t graph is the displacement. So the displacement is the area under a straight line — and that is a shape we can handle with school geometry.

Look at the picture. The straight line starts at height u on the v-axis and rises to height v at time t. The area beneath it is a trapezium, and rather than fight it as one shape, we split it. Underneath sits a blue rectangle of width t and height u. On top sits a green right-triangle of base t and height v minus u. Two easy shapes.

So write the area down. The rectangle contributes u times t. The triangle contributes half times base t times height v minus u. Add them, and that sum is the displacement s. Nothing has been assumed here beyond the line being straight.

Now the elegant step. We already have equation one, which says v minus u equals a t. And v minus u is precisely the height of our triangle — look at the red mark on the right of the picture. So substitute it in.
The triangle becomes half times t times a t, which is half a t squared. So s equals u t plus half a t squared. That is equation two, derived from geometry plus one substitution.

And the red note gives you the physical reading, which is what makes this equation memorable rather than a jumble of symbols. The rectangle, u t, is the distance the body would have covered if it had simply cruised at its starting speed the whole time. The triangle, half a t squared, is the extra distance the speeding-up contributed on top of that. Every term is a physical thing, not a symbol.

Notice what just happened at the level of method. This derivation is Sub-topic two's rule — area under v-t is displacement — doing real work. The graphs sub-topic was not a detour before the important formulas. It was the thing that generates them.
Derivation two, और ये मेरी पसंदीदा है क्योंकि इसे कोई नई मशीनरी चाहिए ही नहीं। ये बस उसी को भुनाती है जो आप graphs के बारे में पहले सीख चुके हैं।

शुरुआत इस observation से। हमने अभी साबित किया कि velocity u से v तक linearly चढ़ती है। Linear का मतलब v-t graph एक straight line है। और Sub-topic two से हम जानते हैं कि v-t graph के नीचे का area displacement है। तो displacement एक straight line के नीचे का area है — और ये shape school geometry से संभल जाती है।

Picture देखिए। Straight line v-axis पर height u से शुरू होकर time t पर height v तक चढ़ती है। उसके नीचे का area एक trapezium है, और इसे एक shape की तरह लड़ने के बजाय हम इसे तोड़ देते हैं। नीचे एक blue rectangle है, width t और height u. ऊपर एक green right-triangle है, base t और height v minus u. दो आसान shapes.
तो area लिख डालिए। Rectangle देता है u into t. Triangle देता है half into base t into height v minus u. जोड़िए, और वो sum ही displacement s है। यहाँ line के सीधा होने के अलावा कुछ नहीं माना गया।
अब वो सुंदर step. हमारे पास equation one पहले से है, जो कहती है v minus u equals a t. और v minus u ठीक हमारे triangle की height है — picture में दाईं तरफ़ red mark देखिए। तो इसे रख दीजिए।
Triangle बन जाता है half into t into a t, यानी half a t squared. तो s equals u t plus half a t squared. यही equation two है, geometry और एक substitution से निकली हुई।

और red note आपको physical reading देता है, जो इस equation को symbols के ढेर के बजाय यादगार बनाती है। Rectangle, यानी u t, वो distance है जो body तय करती अगर वो पूरे वक़्त अपनी शुरुआती speed पर ही चलती रहती। Triangle, यानी half a t squared, वो अतिरिक्त distance है जो तेज़ होने ने उसके ऊपर जोड़ा। हर term एक physical चीज़ है, कोई symbol नहीं।

ग़ौर कीजिए method के स्तर पर अभी क्या हुआ। ये derivation Sub-topic two का rule है — area under v-t is displacement — असल काम करते हुए। Graphs वाला sub-topic ज़रूरी formulas से पहले का कोई चक्कर नहीं था। वो वही चीज़ है जो इन formulas को पैदा करती है।

sections.subtopic: Equations of Motion and Free Fall
sections.title: Derivation 3: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, eliminating time

board_events.text: The time-independent form
Reach for this one when $t$ is neither given nor wanted.
Start from the chain rule: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{dv}{ds} \cdot \dfrac{ds}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{ds}$, so $v\,dv = a\,ds$.
WHY THIS STEP: it links velocities directly to displacement, sidestepping time entirely — perfect for stopping-distance problems.
Notice $t$ appears NOWHERE in the result. That absence is the whole point of the equation.

segments.text: Derivation three, and this one exists for a specific and very practical reason. Sometimes a problem gives you speeds and distances and asks for a speed or a distance — and time is neither given nor wanted. Using equations one and two would mean finding t just to throw it away. Equation three skips that entirely.
So the goal is a relation with no t in it. And that tells us what to do: we need to get rid of d t.

The move is a chain rule trick, and it is worth learning properly because Sub-topic five is built entirely on it. Acceleration is d v by d t. Insert d s twice: write d v by d t as d v by d s, times d s by d t. But d s by d t is just v, the velocity. So a equals v times d v by d s. Rearranged: v d v equals a d s. Look at what that achieved — d t has vanished, replaced by d s. We have traded time for position.
Now integrate both sides, with the right limits. On the left, velocity runs from u to v. On the right, displacement runs from zero to s.
Evaluate. The left side is v squared over two minus u squared over two, which is v squared minus u squared, all over two. The right side — constant a again coming out of the integral — is simply a s.
Multiply through by two and rearrange: v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Equation three, and there is no t anywhere in it.

The red note names the payoff. This equation links velocities directly to displacement, sidestepping time entirely. And it is perfect for stopping-distance problems, which is exactly where the exam sends it: a car at some speed, brakes with some deceleration, how far does it travel? No time is mentioned, none is wanted, and equation three answers in one line.

So notice the absence, because absence is the feature here. T appears nowhere in the result. Students memorise three equations as three equally-weighted facts, but they are better understood by what each one leaves out. Equation one has no s. Equation two has all of them but v. Equation three has no t. Match the equation to what the question refuses to give you.

Derivation three, और ये एक ख़ास और बेहद practical वजह से मौजूद है। कभी-कभी problem आपको speeds और distances देती है और speed या distance पूछती है — और time न दिया गया है न चाहिए। Equations one और two इस्तेमाल करने का मतलब होगा t निकालना सिर्फ़ उसे फेंक देने के लिए। Equation three ये पूरा चक्कर छोड़ देती है।
तो मक़सद है ऐसा relation जिसमें t हो ही नहीं। और इससे पता चल जाता है क्या करना है: हमें d t से छुटकारा पाना है।

चाल है chain rule की, और इसे ठीक से सीखिए क्योंकि Sub-topic five पूरा इसी पर खड़ा है। Acceleration है d v by d t. उसमें d s दो बार घुसाइए: d v by d t को लिखिए d v by d s, into d s by d t. मगर d s by d t तो बस v है, velocity. तो a equals v into d v by d s. Rearrange: v d v equals a d s. देखिए इससे क्या हुआ — d t ग़ायब हो गया, उसकी जगह d s आ गया। हमने time का सौदा position से कर लिया।
अब दोनों तरफ़ integrate कीजिए, सही limits के साथ। बाईं तरफ़ velocity u से v तक। दाईं तरफ़ displacement zero से s तक।
Evaluate कीजिए। बायाँ हिस्सा है v squared over two minus u squared over two, यानी v squared minus u squared, बटा two. दायाँ हिस्सा — constant a फिर integral से बाहर आकर — सीधा a s है।
दोनों तरफ़ two से गुणा कीजिए और rearrange: v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Equation three, और इसमें कहीं t है ही नहीं।

Red note फ़ायदा बताता है। ये equation velocities को सीधे displacement से जोड़ती है, time को पूरी तरह किनारे करके। और ये stopping-distance problems के लिए एकदम सही है, और exam इसे ठीक वहीं भेजती है: एक car किसी speed पर, किसी deceleration से brake, कितनी दूर जाएगी? Time न ज़िक्र में है, न चाहिए, और equation three एक line में जवाब दे देती है।

तो उस ग़ैरहाज़िरी पर ग़ौर कीजिए, क्योंकि यहाँ ग़ैरहाज़िरी ही ख़ूबी है। Result में t कहीं नहीं है। Students तीनों equations को बराबर वज़न वाले तीन facts की तरह रटते हैं, मगर इन्हें बेहतर इस बात से समझा जाता है कि हर एक क्या छोड़ देती है। Equation one में s नहीं है। Equation two में v को छोड़कर सब हैं। Equation three में t नहीं है। Equation को उससे मिलाइए जो question आपको देने से इनकार कर रहा है।

For a body starting from REST under constant acceleration, look at the displacement in each successive equal time interval.
That is proportional to $(2n - 1)$ — the odd numbers.

board_events.text: DO NOT confuse this with the TOTAL distance after $n$ seconds, which goes as $n^2$: $1 : 4 : 9$. That confusion is the most common error here.
Distance in the $n$th SECOND is an interval. Distance in $n$ seconds is a running total. Different questions, different answers.

segments.text: One bonus result before we consolidate, and it is a genuinely historic one — the pattern Galileo measured on falling bodies four centuries ago, with nothing but an inclined plane and a water clock.

Here is the question he asked. Take a body starting from rest under constant acceleration. Now do not ask how far it has gone in total — ask how far it travels during each successive second. First second, then second second, then third. Is there a pattern?
There is, and the formula gives it. The displacement during the n-th second, starting from rest, is a over two times the quantity two n minus one. Set n to one, two, three and read off what happens.

The a over two is just a constant multiplier, so the shape of the answer is carried entirely by two n minus one. And two n minus one, as n runs through one, two, three, four, generates one, three, five, seven. The odd numbers.

Look at the picture. Each bar is one second's worth of travel, and they stack up as one unit, three units, five units, seven units. The body covers three times as much ground in its second second as in its first. That is the signature of uniform acceleration, and Galileo spotted it by measurement long before anyone could derive it.
So the ratio to remember is one to three to five to seven, and onward through the odd numbers. It is worth knowing on sight, because N E E T in particular likes asking for it directly.

<whisper>Now the red note, and this is the single most common error in this entire sub-topic. Do not confuse distance in the n-th second with distance in n seconds. The total distance after one, two, three seconds goes as n squared — that is one, four, nine. And in a multiple-choice question, one to four to nine will be sitting right there next to one to three to five, waiting for you.

So hold the distinction by meaning, not by memorising two ratios. Distance in the n-th second is an interval — it asks how much ground was covered during that one second alone. Distance in n seconds is a running total — everything from the start. Different questions entirely. Read which one the exam actually asked before you reach for either ratio.
Consolidate करने से पहले एक bonus result, और ये सच में ऐतिहासिक है — वो pattern जो Galileo ने चार सदी पहले गिरती चीज़ों पर नापा था, सिर्फ़ एक inclined plane और एक water clock के साथ।

उसने सवाल ये पूछा। Rest से शुरू होकर constant acceleration से चलती body लीजिए। अब ये मत पूछिए कि कुल कितना चली — पूछिए कि हर अगले second में कितना चली। पहला second, फिर दूसरा, फिर तीसरा। क्या कोई pattern है?
है, और formula वही देता है। Rest से शुरू करके n-th second में displacement है a over two into quantity two n minus one. N को one, two, three रखिए और देखिए क्या होता है।

वो a over two सिर्फ़ एक constant multiplier है, तो answer की shape पूरी तरह two n minus one उठाए हुए है। और two n minus one, जब n one, two, three, four से गुज़रे, बनाता है one, three, five, seven. यानी odd numbers.

Picture देखिए। हर bar एक second की यात्रा है, और वो one unit, three units, five units, seven units की तरह चढ़ते हैं। Body अपने दूसरे second में पहले second से तिगुनी ज़मीन तय करती है। यही uniform acceleration का हस्ताक्षर है, और Galileo ने इसे नाप से पकड़ा था, इससे बहुत पहले कि कोई इसे derive कर पाता।
तो याद रखने वाला ratio है one to three to five to seven, और आगे odd numbers में। इसे देखते ही पहचानना काम आता है, क्योंकि ख़ासकर N E E T इसे सीधे पूछना पसंद करता है।

<whisper>अब red note, और यही इस पूरे sub-topic की सबसे आम ग़लती है। N-th second में distance को n seconds में distance से मत गड्डमड्ड कीजिए। One, two, three seconds के बाद का total distance n squared की तरह चलता है — यानी one, four, nine. और multiple-choice question में one to four to nine ठीक बग़ल में बैठा होगा, one to three to five के पास, आपका इंतज़ार करता हुआ।

तो इस फ़र्क़ को meaning से पकड़िए, दो ratios रटकर नहीं। N-th second में distance एक interval है — ये पूछता है उस अकेले second में कितनी ज़मीन तय हुई। N seconds में distance एक running total है — शुरू से सब कुछ। बिलकुल अलग सवाल। कोई भी ratio उठाने से पहले पढ़िए exam ने असल में कौन सा पूछा है।

sections.subtopic: Equations of Motion and Free Fall
sections.title: The three equations and their companions

board_events.text: The three equations of motion (uniform acceleration $a$)
$u =$ initial velocity, $v =$ final velocity, $a =$ constant acceleration, $t =$ time elapsed, $s =$ displacement. All SI: m/s, m/s$^2$, s, m.

board_events.latex: s_{n\text{th}} = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1) \quad \text{(displacement during the } n\text{th second)}

board_events.text: Pick your equation by what the question WITHHOLDS: (1) has no $s$, (2) has no $v$, (3) has no $t$.
All three require CONSTANT acceleration. Variable $a$ makes them invalid — not approximate. Invalid.

segments.text: Now the consolidation. Here are the three equations of motion, for uniform acceleration a, gathered where you can see them together.
Equation one: v equals u plus a t. Velocity, acceleration, time. Derived from the definition of acceleration in two lines.
Equation two: s equals u t plus half a t squared. Displacement, initial velocity, acceleration, time. Derived from the area under the v-t graph.
Equation three: v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Velocities, acceleration, displacement. Derived by eliminating time through the chain rule.

The symbols, so nothing is ambiguous. U is initial velocity, v is final velocity, a is the constant acceleration, t is time elapsed, and s is displacement — displacement, note, not distance. Everything in S I: metres per second, metres per second squared, seconds, metres. And because s is a displacement, it carries a sign, exactly as it did in Sub-topic one.

Two companions worth having. First, the average-velocity form: s equals u plus v over two, times t. Read it — that is average velocity times time, and for uniform acceleration the average of the velocity is simply the average of the endpoints. It is often the fastest route when you know both velocities and the time.

Second, displacement during the n-th second: u plus a over two times two n minus one. Note this general version keeps u, so it works for a body that did not start from rest. Set u to zero and you recover Galileo's odd numbers.

Now the red note, and this is the strategy that turns four formulas into one decision. Pick your equation by what the question withholds. Equation one has no s in it. Equation two has no v. Equation three has no t. So find the quantity the problem neither gives you nor asks for, and use the equation that does not contain it. That single habit removes almost all the flailing.

And the second red note repeats the stamp, because it must be repeated. All three require constant acceleration. If a varies, these are not approximate — they are invalid. There is no partial credit in physics for using a formula outside its domain, and the exam knows this well enough to test it directly.
अब consolidation. यहाँ हैं तीनों equations of motion, uniform acceleration a के लिए, एक साथ जहाँ आप इन्हें देख सकें।
Equation one: v equals u plus a t. Velocity, acceleration, time. Acceleration की definition से दो lines में निकली।
Equation two: s equals u t plus half a t squared. Displacement, initial velocity, acceleration, time. V-t graph के नीचे के area से निकली।
Equation three: v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Velocities, acceleration, displacement. Chain rule से time हटाकर निकली।

Symbols, ताकि कुछ धुँधला न रहे। U है initial velocity, v है final velocity, a है constant acceleration, t है time elapsed, और s है displacement — displacement, ग़ौर कीजिए, distance नहीं। सब कुछ S I में: metres per second, metres per second squared, seconds, metres. और चूँकि s एक displacement है, वो sign रखता है, बिलकुल जैसे Sub-topic one में रखता था।

दो companions रखने लायक़ हैं। पहला, average-velocity form: s equals u plus v over two, into t. पढ़िए — ये average velocity into time है, और uniform acceleration के लिए velocity का average बस endpoints का average होता है। जब दोनों velocities और time पता हों, ये अक्सर सबसे तेज़ रास्ता है।

दूसरा, n-th second में displacement: u plus a over two into two n minus one. ग़ौर कीजिए ये general version u रखता है, तो ये उस body पर भी चलेगा जो rest से शुरू नहीं हुई। U को zero रखिए और Galileo के odd numbers वापस मिल जाते हैं।

अब red note, और यही वो strategy है जो चार formulas को एक फ़ैसले में बदल देती है। अपनी equation उससे चुनिए जो question आपसे रोक रहा है। Equation one में s नहीं है। Equation two में v नहीं है। Equation three में t नहीं है। तो वो quantity ढूँढिए जो problem न आपको दे रही है न पूछ रही है, और वो equation इस्तेमाल कीजिए जिसमें वो है ही नहीं। ये एक आदत लगभग सारी छटपटाहट ख़त्म कर देती है।

और दूसरा red note वही stamp दोहराता है, क्योंकि इसे दोहराना ज़रूरी है। तीनों को constant acceleration चाहिए। अगर a बदलता है, तो ये approximate नहीं हैं — ये invalid हैं। Physics में formula को उसके दायरे के बाहर इस्तेमाल करने पर कोई part marks नहीं मिलते, और exam इसे इतना अच्छे से जानती है कि सीधे यही test करती है।

sections.subtopic: Equations of Motion and Free Fall
sections.title: Free-fall forms, odd numbers, and stopping distance

board_events.text: Substitute $a = \pm g$, with a chosen sign convention
DROPPED FROM REST (taking DOWN as positive):
THROWN UP with speed $u$ (taking UP as positive, so $a = -g$):
Stopping distance grows with the SQUARE of speed. Double the speed, QUADRUPLE the distance.
These are not new equations — every one is the three equations with $a$ replaced by $g$ and a convention applied.

segments.text: Now the free-fall forms, and I want to frame these correctly before we list them, because students file them away as a separate set of formulas to memorise. They are not. Every single one is the three equations with a replaced by g, and a sign convention applied. If you ever forget one, you can regenerate it in ten seconds.
First case: dropped from rest, taking down as positive. Down positive means g is plus, and dropped means u is zero. Watch what happens to the three equations under those two substitutions.

Equation one, v equals u plus a t, loses its u and becomes v equals g t. Equation two, s equals u t plus half a t squared, loses its first term and becomes h equals half g t squared. Equation three, v squared equals u squared plus two a s, loses u squared and becomes v squared equals two g h. Three equations, three deletions, done. Nothing memorised.
Second case: thrown up with speed u, taking up as positive, so a is minus g. Now the results are about the flight.

Maximum height is u squared over two g — that comes from equation three, setting the final velocity to zero at the top. Time to the top is u over g, from equation one, same condition. And total flight time back to the start is two u over g, by the symmetry we established: equal time up and down, so double the time up. Each one is a one-line consequence.
Galileo's odd numbers, back on the sheet where you can find them: from rest, the successive-second displacements go one, three, five, seven, and onward.

And stopping distance. From equation three with the final velocity zero: d equals v naught squared over two a. And read the shape of that — d is proportional to v naught squared. The relationship is quadratic, not linear.

<whisper>The red note is the exam's favourite consequence of that. Stopping distance grows with the square of speed. Double your speed and you do not double your stopping distance — you quadruple it. Triple it and you get nine times. This is not just an exam trick, it is why highway speed limits matter so much: a small rise in speed inflates the stopping distance disproportionately.

So take the framing with you. These are not new equations. Every one is the three equations with a replaced by g and a convention applied. Memorise the three, know your convention, and this entire list regenerates itself whenever you need it.

अब free-fall forms, और इन्हें गिनाने से पहले मैं सही framing देना चाहती हूँ, क्योंकि students इन्हें रटने के लिए एक अलग set मान लेते हैं। ये नहीं हैं। इनमें से हर एक वही तीन equations हैं, बस a की जगह g और एक sign convention लगाकर। अगर कोई भूल जाएँ, तो दस seconds में दोबारा बना सकते हैं।
पहला case: rest से गिराई गई, down को positive मानकर। Down positive यानी g plus है, और गिराई गई यानी u zero है। इन दो substitutions में तीनों equations का क्या होता है, देखिए।

Equation one, v equals u plus a t, अपना u खोकर बन जाती है v equals g t. Equation two, s equals u t plus half a t squared, अपना पहला term खोकर बन जाती है h equals half g t squared. Equation three, v squared equals u squared plus two a s, अपना u squared खोकर बन जाती है v squared equals two g h. तीन equations, तीन कटौतियाँ, हो गया। कुछ रटा नहीं गया।
दूसरा case: speed u से ऊपर फेंकी गई, up को positive मानकर, तो a है minus g. अब results flight के बारे में हैं।

Maximum height है u squared over two g — ये equation three से आती है, ऊपर final velocity zero रखकर। ऊपर तक का time है u over g, equation one से, वही condition. और वापस शुरुआत तक का total flight time है two u over g, उसी symmetry से जो हमने बनाई: time up बराबर time down, तो time up का दुगना। हर एक एक line का नतीजा है।
Galileo के odd numbers, वापस sheet पर जहाँ आप उन्हें ढूँढ सकें: rest से, हर अगले second के displacements चलते हैं one, three, five, seven, और आगे।

और stopping distance. Equation three से, final velocity zero रखकर: d equals v naught squared over two a. और इसकी shape पढ़िए — d, v naught squared के proportional है। ये relationship quadratic है, linear नहीं।

<whisper>Red note उसी का वो नतीजा है जो exam को सबसे प्यारा है। Stopping distance speed के square के साथ बढ़ता है। Speed दुगनी कीजिए और stopping distance दुगना नहीं होता — चौगुना होता है। तिगुनी कीजिए तो नौ गुना। ये सिर्फ़ exam trick नहीं है, यही वजह है कि highway speed limits इतनी मायने रखती हैं: speed में ज़रा सी बढ़त stopping distance को बेतहाशा फुला देती है।
तो framing साथ ले जाइए। ये नई equations नहीं हैं। हर एक वही तीन equations हैं, a की जगह g और एक convention लगाकर। तीन याद रखिए, अपना convention जानिए, और ये पूरी list जब चाहिए तब ख़ुद बन जाएगी।

<text x="240" y="262" font-size="11" font-weight="bold">v = 0 + (10)(3) = 30 m/s</text>
<text x="40" y="262" font-size="11">Only ONE unknown at a time — find t first, then feed it into v = u + gt.</text>
</g></svg>

board_events.text: GIVEN: $u = 0$ (dropped, not thrown), $h = 45$ m, $g = 10$ m/s$^2$. Take DOWNWARD as positive.
(a) Time to reach the ground. Use $h = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $u = 0$.
(b) Velocity just before impact. Now feed that $t$ into $v = u + gt$.
Reject the negative root $t = -3$ s: it is the time BEFORE the drop, which the algebra politely offers and the physics forbids.

segments.text: A board-level example, and the cleanest possible free-fall problem. A ball is dropped from rest from the top of a forty five metre tall building. Taking g as ten and ignoring air resistance, find the time it takes to reach the ground and its velocity just before impact.

Look at the picture. Down has been taken as positive — that is step one, before anything else. And notice why that choice is convenient here: the ball starts at the top and everything happens downward, so every quantity in this problem will come out positive. No minus signs to slip on.

So the given data. U is zero — the word is dropped, not thrown, and that single word is worth a mark. Dropped means released from rest. H is forty five metres. G is ten metres per second squared, positive because down is positive.

Part a, the time. Which equation? Ask what the problem withholds: we have no final velocity and are not asked for one yet. So use equation two, s equals u t plus half a t squared, which is the one with no v in it.

Substitute. U is zero so the first term vanishes entirely, and we get forty five equals half times ten times t squared, which is five t squared. So t squared is nine, and t is three seconds. Notice how little work that was — the whole equation collapsed the moment u went to zero.
Part b, the impact velocity. Now we have t, so equation one is the easy route: v equals u plus g t.

Substitute: v equals zero plus ten times three, which is thirty metres per second, downward. And the sign is a real result, not decoration — positive means downward, because that is the convention we fixed at the start. Note also the method: find one unknown at a time, then feed it forward. We got t first, then used it to get v.

One thing worth flagging in the red note. T squared equals nine strictly gives t equals plus or minus three. The algebra politely offers you minus three seconds — the time before the drop, when the ball would have been rising up to the roof if it had always been in free fall. It is a real root of the mathematics and a nonsense answer in the physics. Reject it. This habit of testing roots against the physics is exactly what the harder examples in this sub-topic will demand.

एक board-level example, और free fall की सबसे साफ़ possible problem. एक ball forty five metre ऊँची building की चोटी से rest से गिराई जाती है। G को ten मानकर और air resistance छोड़कर, ज़मीन तक पहुँचने का time और टकराने से ठीक पहले की velocity निकालिए।

Picture देखिए। Down को positive माना गया है — यही step one है, बाक़ी सब से पहले। और ग़ौर कीजिए ये चुनाव यहाँ क्यों सुविधाजनक है: ball ऊपर से शुरू होती है और सब कुछ नीचे की तरफ़ होता है, तो इस problem की हर quantity positive आएगी। कोई minus sign फिसलने के लिए है ही नहीं।

तो given data. U है zero — शब्द है dropped, thrown नहीं, और वो एक शब्द एक mark का है। Dropped का मतलब rest से छोड़ा गया। H है forty five metres. G है ten metres per second squared, positive क्योंकि down positive है।

Part a, time. कौन सी equation? पूछिए problem क्या रोक रही है: हमारे पास final velocity नहीं है और अभी वो पूछी भी नहीं गई। तो equation two इस्तेमाल कीजिए, s equals u t plus half a t squared, जिसमें v है ही नहीं।

Substitute कीजिए। U zero है तो पहला term पूरी तरह ग़ायब, और मिलता है forty five equals half into ten into t squared, यानी five t squared. तो t squared है nine, और t है three seconds. ग़ौर कीजिए कितना कम काम था — u के zero होते ही पूरी equation सिमट गई।
Part b, impact velocity. अब हमारे पास t है, तो equation one आसान रास्ता है: v equals u plus g t.

Substitute: v equals zero plus ten into three, यानी thirty metres per second, downward. और वो sign एक असली result है, सजावट नहीं — positive का मतलब downward, क्योंकि यही convention हमने शुरू में fix की थी। Method भी ग़ौर कीजिए: एक बार में एक unknown निकालिए, फिर उसे आगे बढ़ाइए। पहले t मिला, फिर उससे v.

Red note में एक बात बताने लायक़ है। T squared equals nine सख़्ती से t equals plus या minus three देता है। Algebra आपको शराफ़त से minus three seconds पेश करता है — drop से पहले का time, जब ball छत तक उठ रही होती अगर वो हमेशा free fall में रही होती। ये mathematics की असली root है और physics में बेतुका answer। इसे reject कीजिए। Roots को physics के ख़िलाफ़ जाँचने की यही आदत इस sub-topic के कठिन examples में माँगी जाएगी।

board_events.text: Stops in distance $d$ from speed $v$. From $2v$, same deceleration, it stops in:

<text x="220" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold">4d — four times, not twice</text>
<rect x="40" y="170" width="190" height="34" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="1"/>
<text x="50" y="191" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">TRAP: "double v, double d" → 2d</text>
<rect x="240" y="170" width="190" height="34" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="1"/>
<text x="250" y="191" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">d = v²/2a, so d ∝ v² → 4d</text>
<text x="235" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5">From v² = u² + 2as with final velocity zero: d = v² / 2a.</text>

board_events.text: OPTIONS: (A) $d$  (B) $2d$  (C) $3d$  (D) $4d$
THE TRAP: 'double the speed $\to$ double the distance', so $2d$. That linear instinct is wrong.
Braking distance grows with the SQUARE of speed, not in proportion to it.

board_events.latex: v^2 = u^2 + 2as \text{ with final velocity } 0 \;\Rightarrow\; d = \frac{v^2}{2a} \propto v^2

board_events.text: SPEED CUE: whenever you see 'speed doubled/tripled, same braking', jump straight to $d \propto v^2$. No numbers needed.

segments.text: A N E E T speed trap, and this one is worth the time because it is both a reliable exam question and a fact that matters outside the exam hall. A car braking at a fixed deceleration stops in a distance d from a speed v. If it instead approaches at twice v, with the same deceleration, its stopping distance is what?

Look at the picture. The blue bar is the stopping distance at speed v. The red bar below is the stopping distance at twice v, drawn to scale. Look at how much longer it is. That length is the whole answer, and it is already obviously not double.
The options are d, two d, three d, and four d. And two d is sitting there in position B, waiting.

Here is the trap, in the red note. Double the speed, double the distance — so two d. That is a linear instinct, and linear instincts are usually right in everyday life, which is exactly why this one fools people. But braking distance is not linear in speed.
Braking distance grows with the square of speed. And that is not a fact to memorise on its own — it falls directly out of equation three, which is the whole reason equation three exists.

Watch. Take v squared equals u squared plus two a s, and set the final velocity to zero, because the car stops. That gives the stopping distance d equals v squared over two a. Now read the structure rather than the numbers: a is fixed, since the brakes are the same. So d is proportional to v squared. That is the physics; everything else is arithmetic.

So doubling v multiplies d by two squared, which is four. The answer is D, four d. And notice we never needed an actual speed, an actual deceleration, or an actual distance. The proportionality did all the work.

<whisper>The speed cue, and this is what wins the mark under time pressure. Whenever you see the words 'speed doubled or tripled, same braking', do not set up equations. Jump straight to d is proportional to v squared and square the factor. Doubled goes to four times, tripled goes to nine times. And carry the real-world reading with you too: this is exactly why highway speed limits matter so much. A small rise in speed inflates the stopping distance disproportionately, and that is a physics fact with consequences well beyond a mark on a paper.

एक N E E T speed trap, और ये वक़्त देने लायक़ है क्योंकि ये भरोसेमंद exam question भी है और exam hall के बाहर मायने रखने वाला fact भी। एक car किसी fixed deceleration पर brake लगाकर speed v से distance d में रुकती है। अगर वो दुगनी speed पर आए, उसी deceleration के साथ, तो stopping distance क्या होगा?

Picture देखिए। Blue bar speed v पर stopping distance है। नीचे red bar दुगनी v पर stopping distance है, scale में खींचा हुआ। देखिए कितना लंबा है। वो लंबाई ही पूरा answer है, और ये पहले से ही साफ़ दिख रहा है कि दुगना नहीं है।
Options हैं d, two d, three d, और four d. और two d वहीं position B पर बैठा इंतज़ार कर रहा है।

Trap ये है, red note में। Speed दुगनी, तो distance दुगना — यानी two d. ये linear instinct है, और रोज़मर्रा की ज़िंदगी में linear instincts आमतौर पर सही होते हैं, इसीलिए ये वाला लोगों को बेवक़ूफ़ बनाता है। मगर braking distance speed में linear नहीं है।
Braking distance speed के square के साथ बढ़ता है। और ये अलग से रटने वाला fact नहीं है — ये सीधा equation three से निकलता है, और equation three का पूरा वजूद ही इसी के लिए है।

देखिए। V squared equals u squared plus two a s लीजिए, और final velocity zero रखिए, क्योंकि car रुक जाती है। इससे मिलता है stopping distance d equals v squared over two a. अब numbers के बजाय structure पढ़िए: a fixed है, क्योंकि brakes वही हैं। तो d, v squared के proportional है। यही physics है; बाक़ी सब arithmetic है।
तो v दुगनी करने पर d, two squared यानी four से गुणा होता है। Answer है D, four d. और ग़ौर कीजिए हमें न कोई असली speed चाहिए थी, न deceleration, न distance. सारा काम proportionality ने किया।

<whisper>Speed cue, और time pressure में mark यही दिलाता है। जब भी शब्द दिखें 'speed doubled या tripled, same braking', equations मत लगाइए। सीधे d is proportional to v squared पर कूदिए और factor का square कीजिए। दुगना यानी चार गुना, तिगुना यानी नौ गुना। और असली दुनिया वाली reading भी साथ ले जाइए: यही वजह है कि highway speed limits इतनी मायने रखती हैं। Speed में ज़रा सी बढ़त stopping distance को बेतहाशा फुला देती है, और ये physics का ऐसा fact है जिसके नतीजे काग़ज़ के एक mark से कहीं आगे जाते हैं।

board_events.text: SETUP: take UP as positive, origin at the launch point. Then $u = +20$, $a = -10$, and the GROUND is at $s = -25$ m.
(a) Max height above the launch point: at the top $v = 0$, so use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

board_events.latex: 0 = 20^2 - 2(10)H \Rightarrow H = 20 \text{ m above the tower top}; \quad \text{above ground} = 25 + 20 = 45 \text{ m}

board_events.text: The negative root $t = -1$ s is discarded as unphysical — it is the 'time before launch' the maths politely offers.

segments.text: J E E Main level, and this is where the sign convention stops being a lecture and starts being the whole problem. From the top of a twenty five metre tower, a stone is thrown vertically upward at twenty metres per second. Find the maximum height above the ground, the total time before it hits the ground, and its speed on impact.

Look at the picture, because the geometry is the difficulty here. The stone does not just go up and come back to your hand. It rises above the launch point, then falls past it, down the side of the tower, all the way to the ground. So the launch point is not the lowest point of the motion, and that is what students mishandle.

Set it up carefully. Take up as positive, with the origin at the launch point — the top of the tower. Then u is plus twenty. A is minus ten, because gravity points down and down is now negative. And here is the crucial line: the ground is at s equals minus twenty five metres. Negative, because the ground is below our origin. Get that minus sign right and the problem solves itself. Get it wrong and nothing downstream can be saved.

Part a, maximum height. At the top the velocity is momentarily zero — the condition we established in the symmetry section. We have u, we have a, we want a displacement, and time is neither given nor wanted, so equation three is the tool.

Zero equals twenty squared minus two times ten times H, so H is four hundred over twenty, which is twenty metres above the tower top. But read the question again — it asked for height above the ground. So add the tower: twenty five plus twenty is forty five metres. That final addition is a mark, and it is a mark students routinely leave on the table by answering the question they solved instead of the question that was asked.

Part b, the total time. Use equation two for the position: s equals twenty t minus five t squared. Set s to minus twenty five, because that is where the ground is. Rearranged, that gives t squared minus four t minus five equals zero, which factorises as t minus five, times t plus one. So t equals five seconds.

Part c, impact speed. Equation three again, with s equals minus twenty five. V squared equals four hundred minus two times ten times minus twenty five. Watch that double negative: minus two times ten times minus twenty five is plus five hundred. So v squared is nine hundred and v is thirty metres per second, downward. If you had slipped the sign on s here, you would have got four hundred minus five hundred — a negative v squared, which is the physics telling you loudly that your convention broke.

And the red note handles the other root. T equals minus one second comes out of the quadratic honestly, and it is unphysical — it is the time before launch, when the stone would have been rising toward your hand had it always been in flight. The maths politely offers it. You politely decline.

J E E Main level, और यहीं sign convention lecture होना छोड़कर पूरी problem बन जाती है। एक twenty five metre tower की चोटी से एक stone twenty metres per second पर सीधा ऊपर फेंका जाता है। ज़मीन से maximum height, ज़मीन पर गिरने तक का total time, और टकराने की speed निकालिए।

Picture देखिए, क्योंकि यहाँ मुश्किल geometry ही है। Stone सिर्फ़ ऊपर जाकर आपके हाथ में वापस नहीं आता। वो launch point से ऊपर उठता है, फिर उसके नीचे से गुज़रता है, tower के बग़ल से, सीधे ज़मीन तक। तो launch point motion का सबसे नीचला point नहीं है, और यहीं students गड़बड़ करते हैं।

Setup ध्यान से कीजिए। Up को positive लीजिए, origin launch point पर — tower की चोटी। तो u है plus twenty. A है minus ten, क्योंकि gravity नीचे है और नीचे अब negative है। और यही अहम line है: ज़मीन है s equals minus twenty five metres पर। Negative, क्योंकि ज़मीन हमारे origin के नीचे है। वो minus sign सही कर लीजिए और problem ख़ुद हल हो जाती है। ग़लत कर दीजिए और आगे कुछ नहीं बचाया जा सकता।

Part a, maximum height. ऊपर velocity एक पल के लिए zero है — वही condition जो हमने symmetry वाले section में बनाई थी। हमारे पास u है, a है, हमें displacement चाहिए, और time न दिया गया न चाहिए, तो equation three ही औज़ार है।

Zero equals twenty squared minus two into ten into H, तो H है four hundred over twenty, यानी tower की चोटी से twenty metres ऊपर। मगर question दोबारा पढ़िए — उसने ज़मीन से height पूछी थी। तो tower जोड़िए: twenty five plus twenty, यानी forty five metres. वो आख़िरी जोड़ एक mark है, और students ये mark अक्सर यूँ ही छोड़ आते हैं क्योंकि वो उस सवाल का जवाब देते हैं जो उन्होंने हल किया, उस सवाल का नहीं जो पूछा गया था।

Part b, total time. Position के लिए equation two: s equals twenty t minus five t squared. S को minus twenty five रखिए, क्योंकि ज़मीन वहीं है। Rearrange करने पर मिलता है t squared minus four t minus five equals zero, जो factorise होता है t minus five, into t plus one. तो t equals five seconds.

Part c, impact speed. फिर equation three, s equals minus twenty five के साथ। V squared equals four hundred minus two into ten into minus twenty five. उस double negative पर ग़ौर कीजिए: minus two into ten into minus twenty five है plus five hundred. तो v squared है nine hundred और v है thirty metres per second, downward. अगर आपसे यहाँ s का sign फिसल जाता, तो आते four hundred minus five hundred — यानी negative v squared, जो physics ज़ोर से बता रही होती कि आपका convention टूट गया।

और red note दूसरी root संभालता है। T equals minus one second quadratic से ईमानदारी से निकलती है, और वो unphysical है — वो launch से पहले का time है, जब stone आपके हाथ की तरफ़ उठ रहा होता अगर वो हमेशा उड़ान में रहा होता। Maths शराफ़त से पेश करती है। आप शराफ़त से मना कर दीजिए।

sections.title: Example 4 [JEE Advanced]: the last second of a fall

board_events.text: Dropped from rest from height $H$; the LAST second covers $\tfrac{9}{25}$ of $H$. Find $T$ and $H$.

board_events.text: REASONING: 'last second' means the interval from $(T-1)$ to $T$, where $T$ is the TOTAL fall time. Express that interval's distance as a fraction of the whole.
Notice $g$ cancels completely. The ratio is pure geometry of the timing.
The rejected root is smaller than 1 s, so 'the last second' would not even EXIST. Always test roots against the physics, not just the algebra.

segments.text: J E E Advanced level, and this is the sub-topic's final boss. A ball is dropped from rest from a height H. During the last second of its fall it covers nine twenty fifths of the total height H. Taking g as ten, find the total time of fall and the height H.

Look at the picture, because the entire difficulty is in reading the phrase 'the last second'. It does not mean the first second. It does not mean any particular numbered second. It means the interval from T minus one to T, where T is the total fall time — and T is precisely what we do not know yet. That is what makes this hard: the interval is defined in terms of the unknown.

So read the red note and let it do the work. Last second means the interval from T minus one to T. And the strategy follows: express that interval's distance as a fraction of the whole, then set that fraction to nine twenty fifths.

Build it. From rest, the distance fallen in any time t is half g t squared. So by time T the ball has fallen half g T squared — that is H. By time T minus one it had fallen half g times T minus one, squared. The distance covered during the last second is the difference of those two. Divide by H and you have the fraction. Simplify and the whole thing collapses to two T minus one, over T squared.

Now pause and notice something lovely. G cancelled completely. It appears in the numerator and the denominator and vanishes. So this ratio does not depend on gravity at all — it would be the same on the Moon. The fraction is pure geometry of the timing, and if a question asked only for T, you would not even need the value of g.

Set the fraction equal to nine twenty fifths. Cross-multiply: twenty five times two T minus one equals nine T squared. Rearrange into standard form: nine T squared minus fifty T plus twenty five equals zero.

Quadratic formula. T equals fifty plus or minus the square root of two thousand five hundred minus nine hundred, all over eighteen. Under the root is one thousand six hundred, whose square root is forty. So T equals fifty plus or minus forty, over eighteen — giving either five seconds, or five ninths of a second.
Take T as five and find H: half times ten times twenty five, which is one hundred twenty five metres. Done.

<whisper>But the red note is the real lesson, and it is why this is an Advanced problem rather than an arithmetic one. Why did we reject five ninths of a second? Not because it is small or ugly. Because it is less than one second — and if the entire fall lasted less than a second, then 'the last second' of the fall would not exist. The premise of the question would be meaningless. The algebra handed you a perfectly valid root that the physics forbids. Always test your roots against the physics, not just against the algebra.

J E E Advanced level, और यही इस sub-topic का final boss है। एक ball height H से rest से गिराई जाती है। गिरने के आख़िरी second में वो कुल height H का nine twenty fifths तय करती है। G को ten मानकर, गिरने का total time और height H निकालिए।

Picture देखिए, क्योंकि पूरी मुश्किल 'the last second' पढ़ने में है। इसका मतलब पहला second नहीं है। किसी ख़ास number वाला second भी नहीं। मतलब है T minus one से T तक का interval, जहाँ T कुल fall time है — और T ठीक वही है जो हमें अभी पता नहीं। यही इसे कठिन बनाता है: interval की परिभाषा ही unknown पर टिकी है।

तो red note पढ़िए और उसे काम करने दीजिए। Last second यानी T minus one से T तक का interval. और strategy निकल आती है: उस interval की distance को पूरे का अंश बनाकर लिखिए, फिर उस अंश को nine twenty fifths के बराबर रखिए।

बनाइए। Rest से, किसी भी time t में गिरी distance है half g t squared. तो time T तक ball गिर चुकी है half g T squared — यही H है। Time T minus one तक वो गिरी थी half g into T minus one, squared. आख़िरी second में तय distance इन दोनों का फ़र्क़ है। H से भाग दीजिए और अंश मिल गया। Simplify कीजिए और पूरी चीज़ सिमटकर बन जाती है two T minus one, बटा T squared.

अब ठहरिए और कुछ ख़ूबसूरत देखिए। G पूरी तरह cancel हो गया। वो numerator में भी है और denominator में भी, और ग़ायब हो जाता है। तो ये ratio gravity पर depend ही नहीं करता — ये Moon पर भी वही होता। ये अंश सिर्फ़ timing की geometry है, और अगर question सिर्फ़ T पूछता, तो आपको g की value की ज़रूरत ही नहीं पड़ती।

अंश को nine twenty fifths के बराबर रखिए। Cross-multiply: twenty five into two T minus one equals nine T squared. Standard form में rearrange: nine T squared minus fifty T plus twenty five equals zero.

Quadratic formula. T equals fifty plus या minus square root of two thousand five hundred minus nine hundred, बटा eighteen. Root के नीचे है one thousand six hundred, जिसका square root है forty. तो T equals fifty plus या minus forty, बटा eighteen — जिससे मिलता है या तो five seconds, या five ninths of a second.
T को five लेकर H निकालिए: half into ten into twenty five, यानी one hundred twenty five metres. हो गया।

<whisper>मगर red note ही असली सबक़ है, और इसीलिए ये Advanced problem है, arithmetic नहीं। हमने five ninths of a second को reject क्यों किया? इसलिए नहीं कि वो छोटा या बदसूरत है। इसलिए कि वो one second से कम है — और अगर पूरी fall एक second से कम चलती, तो fall का 'आख़िरी second' होता ही नहीं। Question का आधार ही बेमानी हो जाता। Algebra ने आपको एक बिलकुल जायज़ root थमाई जिसे physics मना करती है। अपनी roots को हमेशा physics के ख़िलाफ़ जाँचिए, सिर्फ़ algebra के ख़िलाफ़ नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Equations of Motion and Free Fall
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: equations of motion and free fall

board_events.text: Five traps, and the first is the cardinal error
1. THE CARDINAL ERROR: using the equations when acceleration isn't constant. If $a$ depends on $t$ or position, the three equations are simply INVALID — go back to calculus.
2. Sign-convention chaos in free fall. Mixing the signs of $u$, $a$ and $s$ wrecks vertical-motion problems. Pick ONE positive direction and apply it to EVERY quantity.

3. Confusing 'distance in the $n$th second' with 'distance in $n$ seconds'. The first is $s_{n\text{th}} = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)$; the second is $s = un + \tfrac{1}{2}an^2$. They are NOT the same number.
4. Believing acceleration is zero at the top of a throw. Velocity is zero there; acceleration is still $g$. The ball doesn't hang weightless — it's about to fall.
5. Mixing $g = 9.8$ and $g = 10$ within one problem. Read which value the question intends and use it consistently.

PRO-TIP: lock in 'up $=$ positive, $a = -g$' for every vertical problem and never re-decide mid-solution. For 'speed doubled/tripled' braking questions, reach for $d \propto v^2$ instead of recomputing.

When you need to find WHEN a body is at a given height, set up the quadratic in $t$ — the two roots are usually the moment it passes that height going UP and again coming DOWN. That is often the whole point of the question.

segments.text: Let us close the most heavily examined sub-topic in this chapter by naming its traps. Five of them, and the first one is in a category of its own.

Trap one, the cardinal error: using the three equations when acceleration is not constant. If a depends on time, or on velocity, or on position, these equations are not slightly off. They are invalid. There is no salvaging the answer. Go back to calculus and integrate from the definitions — which is exactly what Sub-topic five will teach you. Before you write v equals u plus a t, check the stamp on the box.

Trap two: sign-convention chaos in free fall. Mixing the signs of u, a, and s wrecks vertical-motion problems more often than any conceptual misunderstanding. The fix is mechanical: pick one positive direction and apply it to every quantity, together, before you write a single equation. The tower example is the proof — get the ground's minus twenty five right and the problem solves itself.

Trap three: confusing distance in the n-th second with distance in n seconds. The first is u plus a over two times two n minus one — an interval. The second is u n plus half a n squared — a running total. They are not the same number and they are not close. This is the trap behind the one to three to five versus one to four to nine confusion, and it is the most common error in the Galileo material.

Trap four: believing acceleration is zero at the top of a throw. Velocity is zero there. Acceleration is still a full g downward. The ball does not hang weightless at the top — it is about to fall. This is the same zero-velocity trap from Sub-topic one, and free fall is where the exam most loves to set it, because the pause at the top feels so much like nothing is happening.

Trap five, the pure carelessness one: mixing nine point eight and ten inside a single problem. Read which value the question intends, then use it from the first line to the last. Half a solution in each convention gives you a number that is wrong in a way that earns nothing.

Now the pro-tips. Lock in up equals positive, a equals minus g, for every vertical problem, and never re-decide mid-solution. And for any braking question with the words 'speed doubled' or 'speed tripled', do not recompute from scratch — reach straight for d is proportional to v squared and square the factor.

<whisper>And the last one, which is a genuine strategic insight rather than a warning. When you need to find when a body is at a given height, set up the quadratic in t and expect two roots. Do not assume one is wrong. Usually both are real: they are the moment it passes that height going up, and the moment it passes the same height coming back down. That pair is very often the entire point of the question — 'for how long is the ball above forty metres' is asking for the gap between those two roots. Only reject a root when the physics forbids it, as with the negative time, or the fall that was over before its last second could exist.
इस chapter के सबसे ज़्यादा exam होने वाले sub-topic को इसके traps के नाम लेकर बंद करते हैं। पाँच हैं, और पहला अपनी ही श्रेणी में है।

Trap one, cardinal error: तीनों equations को तब इस्तेमाल करना जब acceleration constant नहीं है। अगर a time पर, velocity पर, या position पर depend करता है, तो ये equations थोड़ी सी ग़लत नहीं हैं। ये invalid हैं। Answer बचाया नहीं जा सकता। Calculus पर लौटिए और definitions से integrate कीजिए — Sub-topic five यही सिखाएगा। V equals u plus a t लिखने से पहले डिब्बे पर लगी stamp पढ़िए।

Trap two: free fall में sign-convention की अफ़रातफ़री। U, a, और s के signs मिलाना vertical-motion problems को किसी भी conceptual ग़लतफ़हमी से ज़्यादा बार बर्बाद करता है। इलाज mechanical है: एक positive direction चुनिए और उसे हर quantity पर, एक साथ, एक भी equation लिखने से पहले लगाइए। Tower वाला example सबूत है — ज़मीन का minus twenty five सही कर लीजिए और problem ख़ुद हल हो जाती है।

Trap three: n-th second में distance को n seconds में distance से गड्डमड्ड करना। पहला है u plus a over two into two n minus one — एक interval. दूसरा है u n plus half a n squared — एक running total. ये एक number नहीं हैं और आसपास भी नहीं हैं। यही one to three to five बनाम one to four to nine वाले confusion के पीछे का trap है, और Galileo वाले हिस्से की सबसे आम ग़लती है।

Trap four: ये मानना कि throw के top पर acceleration zero है। Velocity वहाँ zero है। Acceleration अब भी पूरा g downward है। Ball ऊपर weightless लटकती नहीं — वो गिरने ही वाली है। ये वही Sub-topic one वाला zero-velocity trap है, और free fall वो जगह है जहाँ exam इसे सबसे ज़्यादा बिछाना पसंद करती है, क्योंकि ऊपर का वो ठहराव ऐसा लगता है जैसे कुछ हो ही नहीं रहा।

Trap five, शुद्ध लापरवाही वाला: एक ही problem में nine point eight और ten मिलाना। पढ़िए question कौन सी value चाहता है, फिर पहली line से आख़िरी तक वही इस्तेमाल कीजिए। आधा solution एक convention में और आधा दूसरे में — ऐसा number बनता है जो इस तरह ग़लत है कि कुछ नहीं दिलाता।

अब pro-tips. हर vertical problem के लिए lock कीजिए — up equals positive, a equals minus g — और बीच solution में दोबारा फ़ैसला मत कीजिए। और किसी भी braking question में जहाँ 'speed doubled' या 'speed tripled' लिखा हो, शुरू से मत गिनिए — सीधे d is proportional to v squared उठाइए और factor का square कीजिए।

<whisper>और आख़िरी वाला, जो चेतावनी नहीं बल्कि असली रणनीतिक समझ है। जब आपको ढूँढना हो कि body किसी दी हुई height पर कब है, तो t में quadratic बनाइए और दो roots की उम्मीद रखिए। ये मत मान लीजिए कि एक ग़लत है। आमतौर पर दोनों असली होती हैं: एक वो पल जब वो उस height से ऊपर जाते हुए गुज़रती है, और दूसरा जब वही height वापस नीचे आते हुए पार करती है। वो जोड़ी अक्सर पूरे question का मक़सद ही होती है — 'ball कितनी देर forty metres से ऊपर रहती है' असल में उन्हीं दो roots का फ़ासला पूछ रहा है। Root को सिर्फ़ तब reject कीजिए जब physics मना करे, जैसे negative time, या वो fall जो अपने आख़िरी second के होने से पहले ही ख़त्म हो गई।

board_events.text: Two trains crawl out of a station at nearly the same speed. From your window, the other seems FROZEN alongside.
But a person on the platform sees BOTH racing past. Same two trains, same real motion, two different answers.
Velocity is NEVER absolute. It is always measured with respect to a FRAME OF REFERENCE.
When we quote a car's speed as 60 km/h, we silently mean RELATIVE TO THE GROUND. The ground is our default frame — not a privileged one.
Nothing about either train changed between the two descriptions. Only WHO IS WATCHING changed.
This sub-topic makes that dependence explicit, and turns it into a calculating tool.

segments.text: <curious>You are sitting in a train at a station, and the train on the next platform begins to pull out. For a second or two you cannot tell which one is moving — yours or theirs. Everyone has had that moment. This sub-topic is about why that moment is not a mistake of perception. It is physics telling you something true.
Look at the picture. On one side is what you see from your window; on the other is what the platform sees. Same scene, drawn twice, because there are genuinely two answers here.

Two trains crawl out of the station at nearly the same speed, in the same direction. From your window, the other train barely seems to move at all. It sits there beside you, frozen, drifting a few centimetres a minute. That is what you genuinely see, and you are not wrong.

Now look at the person standing on the platform. They see both trains racing past at sixty kilometres per hour. Also not wrong. Same two trains. Same real motion. Two completely different answers to the question 'how fast is that train going?'

So which one is the truth? And the answer physics gives is: both, and the question was badly formed. Read the red note. Velocity is never absolute. It is always, always measured with respect to a frame of reference. Asking how fast something is moving, without saying with respect to what, is like asking whether something is to the left. Left of what?

And here is the thing you have been doing your whole life without noticing. When we say a car's speed is sixty kilometres per hour, we silently mean relative to the ground. Every speed you have quoted, every number in the last three sub-topics, carried that hidden phrase. The ground is our default frame — because we live on it — but it is not a privileged one. Physics does not owe the ground any special status.

So sit with what actually happened between those two descriptions. Nothing about either train changed. Not their speed, not their engines, not one atom. Only who is watching changed. The disagreement is not about the trains at all — it is about the observers.

And that is what makes this sub-topic powerful rather than philosophical. We are going to make that dependence explicit, and then turn it into a calculating tool. Because if you can choose who is watching, you can choose the frame in which a hard problem becomes an easy one.

<curious>आप station पर train में बैठे हैं, और बग़ल वाले platform की train चलना शुरू करती है। एक-दो second के लिए आपको समझ ही नहीं आता कौन सी चल रही है — आपकी या उनकी। ये पल सबने जिया है। ये sub-topic इसी के बारे में है कि वो पल perception की ग़लती नहीं है। वो physics आपको कुछ सच बता रही है।
Picture देखिए। एक तरफ़ वो है जो आपको अपनी खिड़की से दिखता है; दूसरी तरफ़ वो जो platform को दिखता है। वही दृश्य, दो बार खींचा हुआ, क्योंकि यहाँ सच में दो जवाब हैं।

दो trains station से लगभग एक ही speed पर, एक ही direction में निकलती हैं। आपकी खिड़की से दूसरी train हिलती हुई लगती ही नहीं। वो बग़ल में जमी हुई खड़ी है, मिनट में कुछ सेंटीमीटर सरकती हुई। यही आप सच में देखते हैं, और आप ग़लत नहीं हैं।

अब platform पर खड़े आदमी को देखिए। उसे दोनों trains sixty kilometres per hour पर दौड़ती दिखती हैं। वो भी ग़लत नहीं है। वही दो trains. वही असली motion. और 'वो train कितनी तेज़ जा रही है' का जवाब बिलकुल अलग।

तो सच कौन सा है? Physics का जवाब है: दोनों, और सवाल ही ग़लत बना था। Red note पढ़िए। Velocity कभी absolute नहीं होती। वो हमेशा, हमेशा किसी frame of reference के सापेक्ष नापी जाती है। ये पूछना कि कोई चीज़ कितनी तेज़ चल रही है, बिना बताए किसके सापेक्ष, ऐसा है जैसे पूछना कि कोई चीज़ बाईं तरफ़ है क्या। किसके बाईं तरफ़?

और एक बात जो आप ज़िंदगी भर बिना ग़ौर किए करते आए हैं। जब हम कहते हैं car की speed sixty kilometres per hour है, तो हम चुपचाप ground के सापेक्ष कह रहे होते हैं। आपकी बताई हर speed, पिछले तीन sub-topics का हर number, वो छुपा हुआ वाक्यांश साथ लिए हुए था। Ground हमारा default frame है — क्योंकि हम उस पर रहते हैं — मगर वो कोई विशेषाधिकार वाला frame नहीं है। Physics ground को कोई ख़ास दर्जा नहीं देती।

तो ठहरकर देखिए उन दोनों descriptions के बीच असल में क्या हुआ। किसी भी train के बारे में कुछ नहीं बदला। न speed, न engine, न एक परमाणु। सिर्फ़ ये बदला कि कौन देख रहा है। ये असहमति trains के बारे में है ही नहीं — ये observers के बारे में है।

और यही इस sub-topic को दार्शनिक नहीं, ताक़तवर बनाता है। हम इस निर्भरता को साफ़-साफ़ लिखेंगे, और फिर उसे एक calculating tool में बदल देंगे। क्योंकि अगर आप चुन सकते हैं कि कौन देख रहा है, तो आप वो frame चुन सकते हैं जिसमें एक कठिन problem आसान हो जाए।

sections.title: One definition, and the two rules it generates

board_events.text: $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$ — the velocity of A as seen by B
Read it as: the velocity of A AS SEEN BY B. In one dimension the vectors collapse to signed numbers.

board_events.caption: Same individual speeds, wildly different relative speeds

board_events.text: SAME DIRECTION: the speeds partly cancel, so you SUBTRACT. Two riders both at 80 km/h north see each other PARKED.
OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS: the speeds pile up, so you ADD. The same two riders, one north one south, approach at 160 km/h.
Identical individual speeds. Wildly different relative speeds. The difference is entirely in the DIRECTIONS.
You do not memorise 'add' and 'subtract' — both fall out of the one definition once the signs are honest.

segments.text: Everything in this sub-topic comes from one definition, so let us get it on the board and then squeeze it.
The velocity of A relative to B is v A minus v B. That is it. One subtraction. Every rule, every shortcut, every exam trick in this sub-topic is this line wearing different clothes.

Read it out loud in words, because the notation trips people. V A B means the velocity of A as seen by B. The first subscript is the thing being watched; the second is the one doing the watching. And note the arrows on the board are vectors in general — but we are in one dimension, so once you fix a positive direction, they collapse to plain signed numbers. That is the whole simplification our straight line buys us.
Now watch the definition generate the two rules everyone memorises. Look at the picture: two motorcyclists, and in both panels each rides at eighty kilometres per hour. Same speeds throughout.

Left panel, same direction. Both ride north at eighty. So v A B is eighty minus eighty, which is zero. And read what that means physically — each rider sees the other parked alongside, hanging motionless beside them at eighty kilometres an hour. The speeds partly cancel, which is why the rule is 'subtract'.

Right panel, opposite directions. One rides north at eighty, so plus eighty. The other rides south, so with our convention that is minus eighty. Now v A B is eighty minus minus eighty, which is one hundred sixty. Each sees the other approaching at one hundred sixty kilometres per hour. The speeds pile up, which is why the rule is 'add'.

<excited>The red note is the thing worth pausing on. Those two panels have identical individual speeds. Eighty and eighty, both times. And yet the relative speeds are zero and one hundred sixty — as different as two numbers can be. The difference is entirely in the directions. Nothing else changed.

So do not memorise 'same direction subtract, opposite direction add' as two facts. There is only one fact, the definition, and both rules fall out of it automatically the moment your signs are honest. If you sign the velocities properly in the ground frame first, the subtraction does the thinking for you — and the minus times minus becomes a plus without you having to remember any rule at all.
इस sub-topic का सब कुछ एक definition से आता है, तो चलिए उसे board पर लाकर निचोड़ते हैं।
B के सापेक्ष A की velocity है v A minus v B. बस। एक subtraction. इस sub-topic का हर rule, हर shortcut, हर exam trick यही एक line है, अलग-अलग कपड़ों में।

इसे शब्दों में बोलकर पढ़िए, क्योंकि notation लोगों को गिराता है। V A B यानी A की velocity जैसी B को दिखती है। पहला subscript वो चीज़ है जिसे देखा जा रहा है; दूसरा वो जो देख रहा है। और board पर arrows आमतौर पर vectors हैं — मगर हम एक dimension में हैं, तो positive direction fix करते ही वो सीधे signed numbers बन जाते हैं। यही सरलता हमारी straight line हमें देती है।
अब देखिए ये definition कैसे वो दो rules पैदा करती है जो सब रटते हैं। Picture देखिए: दो motorcyclists, और दोनों panels में हर एक eighty kilometres per hour पर चल रहा है। Speeds पूरे वक़्त एक जैसी।

बायाँ panel, same direction. दोनों north में eighty पर। तो v A B है eighty minus eighty, यानी zero. और इसका physical मतलब पढ़िए — हर rider को दूसरा बग़ल में खड़ा दिखता है, eighty kilometres प्रति घंटे पर उसके साथ-साथ जमा हुआ। Speeds आंशिक रूप से cancel होती हैं, इसीलिए rule है 'subtract'.

दायाँ panel, opposite directions. एक north में eighty पर, यानी plus eighty. दूसरा south में, तो हमारी convention से minus eighty. अब v A B है eighty minus minus eighty, यानी one hundred sixty. हर एक को दूसरा one hundred sixty kilometres per hour पर आता दिखता है। Speeds जुड़ जाती हैं, इसीलिए rule है 'add'.

<excited>Red note पर ठहरना बनता है। उन दोनों panels में individual speeds बिलकुल एक जैसी हैं। Eighty और eighty, दोनों बार। और फिर भी relative speeds हैं zero और one hundred sixty — जितने अलग दो numbers हो सकते हैं। पूरा फ़र्क़ directions में है। और कुछ नहीं बदला।

तो 'same direction subtract, opposite direction add' को दो facts की तरह मत रटिए। Fact सिर्फ़ एक है, वो definition, और दोनों rules उससे अपने आप निकल आते हैं जैसे ही आपके signs ईमानदार हों। अगर आप पहले ground frame में velocities को ठीक से sign कर दें, तो subtraction ख़ुद सोच लेता है — और minus into minus बिना किसी rule याद किए plus बन जाता है।
